Our engineering team is implementing improvements across our database and storage infrastructure to ensure that High Availability instances using Regional Persistent Disks recover more rapidly during unplanned outages.
### Google Kubernetes Engine
**Impact:**
The power loss in europe-west2-b caused total zonal failure, autoscaling stalls, API error spikes, and regional pod unavailability across GKE clusters. Total incident duration for GKE was 7 hours and 34 minutes, starting at 23:02 US/Pacific (07:02 BST), reaching initial mitigation at 05:22 US/Pacific (13:22 BST), and achieving final resolution at 06:37 US/Pacific (14:37 BST).

The scale ups in surviving zones were impacted by available capacity. Autoscaling was slowed down due to increased load and failures of underlying APIs, such as Google Compute Engine (see above).
Regional API operations suffered increased failure rates for cluster creation, deletion, updates and node pool operations due to reduced capacity and increased load on underlying APIs (see above).

**Impact:**

**Impact:**

About 45% of instances became unresponsive as Looker's messaging middle tier was unable to recover and reestablish database connectivity due to degraded GKE and Cloud SQL availability.

Subsequently, regional control-plane issues in GKE pushed instance unavailability back to about 35% before settling near 20% for several hours. Engineering teams are working to expand zonal outage telemetry and improve Looker's messaging middleware failovers to shorten recovery times during zonal unavailability.
### AlloyDB
**Impact:**

Regional primary AlloyDB instances experienced up to a 95-minute delay in starting automated failovers due to delayed failover notifications. ~4% of these instances experienced a stalled failover due to Persistent Disk issues that required manual recovery. Additionally, zonal primary instances, zonal secondary instances, and single-node read pool instances encountered downtime directly aligned with the zone's power loss. AlloyDB engineering team will be updating their monitoring system to detect zonal outage reliably and send the failover notification. The AlloyDB team is also partnering with the Persistent Disk team to ensure that high availability instances which leverage regional disk will recover faster during unplanned downtime events.
### BigQuery
**Impact:**
BigQuery experienced a service disruption in the europe-west2 region between 23:03 US/Pacific (07:03 BST) and 04:12 US/Pacific (12:12 BST) (approximately 5 hours and 9 minutes). During this incident, affected customers experienced significant increases in job latencies and high query queuing, resulting in delayed job execution. Customers also experienced intermittent 503 UNAVAILABLE errors on Job API calls (InsertJob, GetQueryResult). Similarly, customers received errors when calling AppendRows on buffered-type streams also after the incident onset until the streams were re-created. Finally, customers experienced reduced processing efficiency and elevated job failure rates across affected projects.
The majority of the impact was confined to customers assigned to the impacted zone and was caused by an autoscaling dependency in a critical data plane job, which was unable to scale up during the failover. Some customers not assigned to the impacted zone saw elevated (1%) error rates on JobAPI calls due to overly broad concurrency throttling in the Job API component.
**Next Steps:**
Engineering teams have updated job provisioning to eliminate the dependency on autoscaling and are enhancing isolation mechanisms for the job server to ensure that future zonal disruptions are contained.
### Memorystore Redis
**Impact:**
During the power disruption, Basic Tier (non-HA) instances located in europe-west2-b experienced full unavailability, while Standard Tier (HA) instances initiated automated failovers or operated in a degraded state with missing replicas.
Following the restoration of the zone, a subset of instances remained stuck in a REPAIRING state. For these affected instances, the data plane remained fully available and online for customer use, but control plane operations such as scaling and RDB exports were temporarily blocked. Google engineers manually mitigated this issue and fully repaired all affected instances within 24 hours.
**Next Steps:**
The team is working on mechanisms to detect cases when the control plane and data plane get out of sync, then reconcile them so that the system can automatically recover.
### Apigee X
**Impact:**
During the power disruption, the Apigee X runtime in the region returned elevated HTTP 5xx errors for 7 hours and 19 minutes. Apigee X is **designed to withstand** a single-zone loss as its datastore keeps replicas across the region's three zones, but a scheduling misconfiguration had placed two of three replicas in the zone that lost power, so the datastore lost quorum and the runtime failed requests instead of failing over.
The errors were concentrated in a small number of affected clusters rather than spread across the region. As remediation, engineers restored the affected replicas into nearby zones. Apigee Hybrid clusters were not severely impacted.
**Next Steps:**
The engineering team has already audited the Apigee fleet to rebalance unevenly spread instances without downtime, and added monitoring to alert if datastore replicas drift across zones. Moving forward, the team will modify Apigee X to strictly enforce that every instance's three datastore replicas always run in three different zones. Additionally, the team is improving alert handling practices to help engineers better focus on affected services during similar outages.
### Apigee Edge
**Impact:**
During the power disruption, Apigee Edge clusters that had a single node in the affected zone successfully auto-recovered once power was restored. However, clusters with multiple nodes in the affected zone experienced extended recovery times. The automated node replacement system didn't handle multiple nodes going down simultaneously. The engineering team will implement retries and scope repository updates to prevent pre-hook timeouts when reaching external OS repositories during the boot process. The team is also investigating further multiple-node failure scenario resilience improvements.
### Cloud Bigtable
**Impact:**
Cloud Bigtable behaved as expected during the europe-west2-b power outage. All single-cluster instances located in europe-west2-b experienced expected zonal unavailability while the zone lost power and recovered. Multi-cluster instances configured with High Availability (HA) routing automatically failed over to healthy replica clusters in other zones where replica clusters and the control plane remained available with sufficient capacity to absorb the failover load.

# Incident Report
## Summary
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 at 22:53 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 06:53 BST), a data center facility that hosts europe-west2-b, a zone within the europe-west2 cloud region, experienced an external electrical power disruption. This resulted in service unavailability for workloads located in this zone. The subsequent failover of these workloads to unaffected zones and alternate regions caused transient latency and elevated error rates across the broader europe-west2 region.
The resolution of the main impact was completed within 6 hours and 8 minutes.
## Root Cause
**Facility architecture and background:**
The data center facility in the UK region hosts Cloud clusters serving the europe-west2-b zone, which form part of the multi-zonal europe-west2 Cloud region. The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture—where the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load—backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC).
Primary utility power is supplied to the facility via two independent feeders (A and B), supplemented by a standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events. The two high-voltage primary feeders (A and B) terminate at separate primary intake switchboards capable of closed-loop operation if either board is taken offline. Switching between the primary and standby utility providers utilizes open transitions and key interlocks to prevent parallel connections across sources.
Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) battery systems provide approximately five minutes of autonomous runtime. This bridge power ensures uninterrupted operation while the PLC detects utility undervoltage events, initiates diesel generator startup, synchronizes the generators, and transfers the site load.
Prior to the utility disruption, the facility had been placed in a temporary single-feed (1N) bridged maintenance posture on the primary utility. Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026. Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while the feed B breaker remained in an open position to allow repairs to be conducted on the B feeder pathway.
**Root Cause:**
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 at 22:53 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 06:53 BST), the primary utility provider experienced an outage on primary utility feed A, caused by an external underground cable fault on the utility network outside the data center facility.
Following the loss of primary utility feed A, a voltage-sensing design flaw and PLC misconfiguration prevented the facility’s generator plant from receiving an automatic start signal to assume the critical load. Consequently, static UPS battery banks sustained the critical load as intended until their reserves were used up, leading to a loss of power across the data halls.
The investigation of the PLC configuration identified the root cause as a misconfiguration of the PLC logic that did not verify both an undervoltage condition and physical breaker position for both utility feeders. Instead, the PLC undervoltage sensing inputs were wired upstream (line side) of the isolated utility feed breakers. The PLC was programmed to verify whether voltage was present on the line side of the feeder before commanding a generator start. At the time of the power event on 19 Oct 2026, the Utility feed B remained energized upstream while its incomer feed was in open position. Consequently, the active and standby master PLCs, which were running identical control logic, sensed live voltage from feed B through shared upstream sensors on the disconnected path. As a result, the PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant.
The onsite facilities team attempted to execute a remote load transfer via the PLC; however, the system inhibited the action due to the live upstream voltage reading on feed B. Recognizing that the UPS battery reserves would be used up before further remote operations could be resolved, the team transferred the facility load to the standby utility source, restoring the critical load that was lost once batteries depleted during this process.
Once utility power was restored via the standby utility source, and UPS batteries started recharging, the onsite facility teams and OEM vendors reconfigured and validated PLC functionality on both undervoltage and breaker status.
Following the initial detection of the power outage, Google engineering teams initiated efforts to address failover issues and lay the groundwork for service restoration. Once the utility feed, UPS systems, and generator capabilities were successfully restored, engineers initiated the recovery procedure to bring europe-west2-b services back online.
## Remediation and Prevention
The sequence of events leading to customer impact was as follows:
* **19 Oct 22:53 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 06:53 BST) -** An electrical power disruption occurred at the data center facility hosting availability zone europe-west2-b, and a PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) startup fault prevented facility emergency generators from assuming the electrical load. Facility load continued to be supported by UPS battery banks until the batteries were depleted.
* **19 Oct 23:00 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 07:00 BST) - Impact start -** As battery backups were used up, physical host servers, local storage infrastructure, and network aggregation hardware in availability zone europe-west2-b lost power, causing instances, database replicas, and worker nodes in that zone to become immediately unreachable.
* **19 Oct 23:04 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 07:04 BST) -** Google engineers were alerted to the disruption via automated monitoring systems and probers, which detected elevated API error ratios, job submission timeouts, and loss of infrastructure reachability in zone europe-west2-b. Engineering teams immediately mobilized to isolate the affected infrastructure and commence recovery.
* **19 Oct 23:09 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 07:09 BST) -** Regional traffic-routing mechanisms and client applications initiated automated failover toward available infrastructure in adjacent availability zones within the region.
* Cross-zone remote procedure calls from regional service control planes directed to metadata and catalog components in the offline zone encountered timeouts, causing initial job submission stalls and API latency spikes.
* The sudden influx of redirected query executions, high-availability database failovers, and compute workloads saturated available compute slots and processing capacity in other availability zones, creating elevated admission queues, delayed database failover completions, and intermittent 500 and 503 API errors across the region.
* **Traffic Isolation:** Google engineers isolated the offline availability zone (europe-west2-b) by adjusting regional service routing away from the affected infrastructure, preventing cross-zone client requests from timing out against offline endpoints.
* **Workload Reprioritization and Resource Safeguards:** Engineers adjusted scheduler allocations and capacity limits across unimpacted infrastructure to prioritize active customer reservations, reduce resource contention on execution slots, and relieve queue backlogs for regional workloads.
* **19 Oct 23:54 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 07:54 BST) - Utility Power Restoration-** Power supply from the standby utility source was restored and power restoration to the data hall began.
* **20 Oct 00:20 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 08:20 BST) - Datahall Power Restoration-** Utility power was re-established to the datahalls. Mains utility power normalized; power feed to data hall verified. Following this, the site operations and engineering teams focused on and completed a reset and tested the emergency backup generator automation controllers to restore facility power.
* **20 Oct 00:40 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 08:40 BST)-** Clusters began to recover, cluster manager systems started rescheduling compute jobs.
* **20 Oct 00:45 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 08:45 BST) -** Network devices were back online.
* **20 Oct 00:50 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 08:50 BST) -** Due to the immediacy of power loss, storage devices with unclean shutdowns began recovery. Responders recognized this and chose not to restore services that would otherwise make this worse. Because of the large volume of storage devices involved, this process required a substantial period to finish prior to restoring service to customers.
* **20 Oct 03:13 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 11:13 BST)-** Power redundancy was verified and the storage infrastructure was sufficiently restored to prepare the initiation of controlled traffic re-admission. The remaining storage systems continued recovery operations.
* **20 Oct 03:45 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 11:45 BST)-** Once system health and storage integrity were verified, engineers executed gradual, controlled traffic re-admission back to zone europe-west2-b allowing accumulated job backlogs to clear smoothly.
* **20 Oct 04:11 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 12:11 BST)-** Google Cloud Platform services and APIs were made fully available to customers. Some Google Compute Engine virtual machines were still not yet available.
* **20 Oct 04:29 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 12:29 BST) -** Regional services and backend compute management systems were fully undrained, marking the end of core platform-level disruption.
* **20 Oct 05:08 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 13:08 BST) - Majority Workload Recovery-** GCE virtual machines were 99.5% operational and healthy, and creating new VMs was fully supported. Service availability was restored for most customer workloads, with resolution confirmed for the majority of users across Google Cloud Platform services in the region. Following the recovery of a small tail of remaining isolated workloads, the closure notification for the incident was posted by 07:03 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 15:03 BST).
Google is committed to preventing a repeat of this issue in the future and is completing the following actions:
**Data Center Action Items:**
* Restoration of normal utility configuration (both A & B feeds) * Utility provider to locate the damaged cable fault, using low-frequency radar penetration testing procedures. **[Completed 26 Oct]** * Utility provider to repair the cable, test and restore the impacted primary utility feed A source. **[Estimated Completion Date 13 Nov]** * Onsite Operations teams with a controlled method of procedure (MOP) to transfer the facility to its primary utility source (feeds A and B) from standby utility feed through coordinated switching with the utility provider **[Estimated Completion Date 17 Nov]**
* Generator confidence testing * Full generator load transfer tests with utility power cutover of the active utility feed. Test automatic startup of generators through PLC signals within the backup battery timer and detailed review of backup procedures **[Completed on 20 Oct and 26 Oct (full critical load transfer test including updated EOPs)]** * Full generator load transfer tests in coordination with the primary utility source feeds (A and B) after restoration work completed by the primary utility provider. **[Estimated Completion Date 17 Nov]**
* PLC configuration fix * Reconfigured and validated the PLC after the outage on 20 Oct and then again on 26 Oct **[Completed 26 Oct]** * Google engineers to work in collaboration with the facility vendor teams to perform a comprehensive PLC code review and system resiliency to multiple failure scenarios. **[Estimated Completion Date (prior to generator transfer test) 06 Nov]** * Validate PLC telemetry once primary utility feed A and B lineup is restored. **[Estimated Completion Date 17 Nov]** * Validate global PLC configurations at sites with similar topologies and PLC manufacturers **[Estimated Completion Date 15 Nov]**
* Emergency Operating Procedures (EOP) documentation update: * Comprehensive update to the EOP for site’s response to unexpected loss of active utility source. Update includes - manual steps to attempt to restore active utility feed, manual restart of generators and manual transfer to other utility sources within the UPS battery run time. **[Completed 26 Oct]** * Ensure updated EOP is practiced twice per shift by on-site facility team. **[Completed 24 Oct and checked with Google DC Operations daily]**
* Detect and prevent future PLC misconfigurations * Google to ensure PLC code reviews are fully conducted and validated during facility commissioning and Integrated System Tests (ISTs) prior to Facility Ready (FR). A second Google team will then validate this within a quarter post-FR. **[Estimated Completion Date 18 Dec]**
* Strengthen change management: * Freeze planned maintenance activities at other sites with similar topologies, and implement elevated approvals and reviews for data center configuration changes which are outside their standard designs. **[Completed Date 30 Oct]**
**Cloud Service Action Items:**
* **Communications Enhancement:** Bolster notification speed by developing an automated alert-to-communication mechanism for location-impacting incidents.
* **Platform Testing:** Expand platform-wide testing outcomes for infrastructure-level events.

# Incident Report
## Summary
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 at 22:53 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 06:53 BST), a data center facility that hosts europe-west2-b, a zone within the europe-west2 cloud region, experienced an external electrical power disruption. This resulted in service unavailability for workloads located in this zone. The subsequent failover of these workloads to unaffected zones and alternate regions caused transient latency and elevated error rates across the broader europe-west2 region.
The resolution of the main impact was completed within 6 hours and 8 minutes.
## Root Cause
**Facility architecture and background:**
The data center facility in the UK region hosts Cloud clusters serving the europe-west2-b zone, which form part of the multi-zonal europe-west2 Cloud region. The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture—where the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load—backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC).
Primary utility power is supplied to the facility via two independent feeders (A and B), supplemented by a standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events. The two high-voltage primary feeders (A and B) terminate at separate primary intake switchboards capable of closed-loop operation if either board is taken offline. Switching between the primary and standby utility providers utilizes open transitions and key interlocks to prevent parallel connections across sources.
Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) battery systems provide approximately five minutes of autonomous runtime. This bridge power ensures uninterrupted operation while the PLC detects utility undervoltage events, initiates diesel generator startup, synchronizes the generators, and transfers the site load.
Prior to the utility disruption, the facility had been placed in a temporary single-feed (1N) bridged maintenance posture on the primary utility. Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026. Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while the feed B breaker remained in an open position to allow repairs to be conducted on the B feeder pathway.
**Root Cause:**
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 at 22:53 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 06:53 BST), the primary utility provider experienced an outage on primary utility feed A, caused by an external underground cable fault on the utility network outside the data center facility.
Following the loss of primary utility feed A, a voltage-sensing design flaw and PLC misconfiguration prevented the facility’s generator plant from receiving an automatic start signal to assume the critical load. Consequently, static UPS battery banks sustained the critical load as intended until their reserves were used up, leading to a loss of power across the data halls.
The investigation of the PLC configuration identified the root cause as a misconfiguration of the PLC logic that did not verify both an undervoltage condition and physical breaker position for both utility feeders. Instead, the PLC undervoltage sensing inputs were wired upstream (line side) of the isolated utility feed breakers. The PLC was programmed to verify whether voltage was present on the line side of the feeder before commanding a generator start. At the time of the power event on 19 Oct 2026, the Utility feed B remained energized upstream while its incomer feed was in open position. Consequently, the active and standby master PLCs, which were running identical control logic, sensed live voltage from feed B through shared upstream sensors on the disconnected path. As a result, the PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant.
The onsite facilities team attempted to execute a remote load transfer via the PLC; however, the system inhibited the action due to the live upstream voltage reading on feed B. Recognizing that the UPS battery reserves would be used up before further remote operations could be resolved, the team transferred the facility load to the standby utility source, restoring the critical load that was lost once batteries depleted during this process.
Once utility power was restored via the standby utility source, and UPS batteries started recharging, the onsite facility teams and OEM vendors reconfigured and validated PLC functionality on both undervoltage and breaker status.
Following the initial detection of the power outage, Google engineering teams initiated efforts to address failover issues and lay the groundwork for service restoration. Once the utility feed, UPS systems, and generator capabilities were successfully restored, engineers initiated the recovery procedure to bring europe-west2-b services back online.
## Remediation and Prevention
The sequence of events leading to customer impact was as follows:
* **19 Oct 22:53 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 06:53 BST) -** An electrical power disruption occurred at the data center facility hosting availability zone europe-west2-b, and a PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) startup fault prevented facility emergency generators from assuming the electrical load. Facility load continued to be supported by UPS battery banks until the batteries were depleted.
* **19 Oct 23:00 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 07:00 BST) - Impact start -** As battery backups were used up, physical host servers, local storage infrastructure, and network aggregation hardware in availability zone europe-west2-b lost power, causing instances, database replicas, and worker nodes in that zone to become immediately unreachable.
* **19 Oct 23:04 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 07:04 BST) -** Google engineers were alerted to the disruption via automated monitoring systems and probers, which detected elevated API error ratios, job submission timeouts, and loss of infrastructure reachability in zone europe-west2-b. Engineering teams immediately mobilized to isolate the affected infrastructure and commence recovery.
* **19 Oct 23:09 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 07:09 BST) -** Regional traffic-routing mechanisms and client applications initiated automated failover toward available infrastructure in adjacent availability zones within the region.
* Cross-zone remote procedure calls from regional service control planes directed to metadata and catalog components in the offline zone encountered timeouts, causing initial job submission stalls and API latency spikes.
* The sudden influx of redirected query executions, high-availability database failovers, and compute workloads saturated available compute slots and processing capacity in other availability zones, creating elevated admission queues, delayed database failover completions, and intermittent 500 and 503 API errors across the region.
* **Traffic Isolation:** Google engineers isolated the offline availability zone (europe-west2-b) by adjusting regional service routing away from the affected infrastructure, preventing cross-zone client requests from timing out against offline endpoints.
* **Workload Reprioritization and Resource Safeguards:** Engineers adjusted scheduler allocations and capacity limits across unimpacted infrastructure to prioritize active customer reservations, reduce resource contention on execution slots, and relieve queue backlogs for regional workloads.
* **19 Oct 23:54 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 07:54 BST) - Utility Power Restoration-** Power supply from the standby utility source was restored and power restoration to the data hall began.
* **20 Oct 00:20 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 08:20 BST) - Datahall Power Restoration-** Utility power was re-established to the datahalls. Mains utility power normalized; power feed to data hall verified. Following this, the site operations and engineering teams focused on and completed a reset and tested the emergency backup generator automation controllers to restore facility power.
* **20 Oct 00:40 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 08:40 BST)-** Clusters began to recover, cluster manager systems started rescheduling compute jobs.
* **20 Oct 00:45 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 08:45 BST) -** Network devices were back online.
* **20 Oct 00:50 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 08:50 BST) -** Due to the immediacy of power loss, storage devices with unclean shutdowns began recovery. Responders recognized this and chose not to restore services that would otherwise make this worse. Because of the large volume of storage devices involved, this process required a substantial period to finish prior to restoring service to customers.
* **20 Oct 03:13 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 11:13 BST)-** Power redundancy was verified and the storage infrastructure was sufficiently restored to prepare the initiation of controlled traffic re-admission. The remaining storage systems continued recovery operations.
* **20 Oct 03:45 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 11:45 BST)-** Once system health and storage integrity were verified, engineers executed gradual, controlled traffic re-admission back to zone europe-west2-b allowing accumulated job backlogs to clear smoothly.
* **20 Oct 04:11 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 12:11 BST)-** Google Cloud Platform services and APIs were made fully available to customers. Some Google Compute Engine virtual machines were still not yet available.
* **20 Oct 04:29 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 12:29 BST) -** Regional services and backend compute management systems were fully undrained, marking the end of core platform-level disruption.
* **20 Oct 05:08 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 13:08 BST) - Majority Workload Recovery-** GCE virtual machines were 99.5% operational and healthy, and creating new VMs was fully supported. Service availability was restored for most customer workloads, with resolution confirmed for the majority of users across Google Cloud Platform services in the region. Following the recovery of a small tail of remaining isolated workloads, the closure notification for the incident was posted by 07:03 US/Pacific (20 Oct 2026, 15:03 BST).

## Detailed Description of Impact
Between Monday, 19 Oct 2026, 23:00 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 07:00 BST) and Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 05:08 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 13:08 BST), customers utilizing Google Cloud Platform services in the europe-west2 region experienced service disruptions across two consecutive phases, lasting a total duration of 6 hours, 08 minutes.
During the initial phase from 23:00 US/Pacific (07:00 BST) to 04:29 US/Pacific (12:29 BST) (duration 5 hours, 29 minutes), customers experienced unavailability of zone-scoped resources in products, including:
* **Compute Engine** - VM instances, zonal MIGs, unmanaged instance groups, zonal NEGs, sole-tenant node groups, zonal reservations, target instances, zonal API operations.
* **Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk** - Zonal PD, zonal Hyperdisk, Hyperdisk storage pools, instant snapshots.
* **GKE -** Zonal clusters (control plane), node pool nodes in -b, PVs on zonal disks.
* **Cloud SQL -** Non-HA instances, read replicas in -b.
* **AlloyDB -** Basic (non-HA) primaries in -b.
* **Bigtable -** Single-cluster instances in -b.
* **Other products with affected zonal resources:** Cloud Batch, Cloud Build, Cloud Storage, Cloud Workstations, Composer, Dataproc, Filestore, Managed Lustre, Migrate to VMs, NetApp Volumes, Pub/Sub Lite, Vertex AI Workbench, VMware Engine.
The unavailability of those resources scoped to a zone that undergoes disruption is working within the design of a zonally-scoped system. Requests made to these resulted either in a timeout or error code during the disruption. Workloads and resources hosted entirely within europe-west2-b became unreachable due to this event.
While the physical power outage was isolated strictly to data center facilities in zone europe-west2-b, some customers running workloads in unimpacted zones (europe-west2-a and europe-west2-c) or across regional architectures also experienced unexpected impact.
Google Cloud designs regional services to be robust to zone failures, but in this case there were a set of unexpected failures which caused impact outside of the zonal failure domain. We are committed to learning from this incident and preventing zonal events from impacting broader regional operations.
The primary causes of impact outside of zone europe-west2-b were:
1) Instantaneous demand surges on neighboring zones (a and c) and
2) Control-plane dependencies across zonal boundaries
See below for more detailed descriptions of impact and next steps for each impacted product.
### Google Compute Engine and Persistent Disk
**Impact:**
Upon power loss in europe-west2-b at 22:53 US/Pacific (06:53 BST), all Compute Engine VMs and zonal Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk volumes in the zone became unavailable. Google Compute Engine's zonal resources, such as VMs, require customers to provision cross-zone failover and recovery mechanisms tailored to their needs. During this incident, however, some of these failover attempts were unsuccessful due to capacity constraints and difficulty in replicating the underlying storage mechanism.
Once data hall power was restored at 00:20 US/Pacific (08:20 BST), engineers worked to confirm storage integrity before restoring compute services. Following platform service restoration, some customer workloads running on Compute Engine instances as well as products that rely on Compute Engine experienced a longer recovery due to action taken by responders in order to prevent data loss. Once storage stabilized, engineers brought VMs and zonal disks in the zone back online between 04:01 US/Pacific (12:01 BST) and 04:29 US/Pacific (12:29 BST). By 04:46 US/Pacific (12:46 BST) new VM creation resumed, and by 05:08 US/Pacific (13:08 BST) over 99% of Compute Engine VM were in a healthy state. (The remaining VMs were restarted after their disks recovered). Any remaining customers that were experiencing VM problems were directed to file a customer support case as per normal procedure.
**Next Steps:**
Google Compute Engine and Persistent Disk engineering teams are conducting a comprehensive postmortem review of this event along with Google data center and infrastructure teams. The follow-up actions focus on preventing a recurrence and on making our clusters recover from an unplanned power loss more quickly and safely. We are also expanding our regular disaster-recovery testing for full cluster power-loss scenarios to validate end-to-end Compute Engine recovery.
The zonal failure in a facility within europe-west2-b exhibited sequencing atypical of previous zonal outages. We are investigating additional signals to incorporate into our failure detection capabilities for Regional Persistent Disk, so that should this sequence recur, Regional Persistent Disk can differentiate this case from the more typical zonal outage scenarios. We exercise caution with all changes to detection mechanisms to ensure we do not regress our capabilities to detect and react to more typical outages.
### Cloud SQL
**Impact:**
Upon power loss, Cloud SQL detected failures and immediately initiated automated failovers for all regional HA instances. The failover was complete for regional instances that did not have Regional Persistent Disk failures (see above), mitigating their impact right away. A majority of the remaining instances recovered by 20 Oct 2026, 01:00 US/Pacific (09:00 BST) once the Regional Persistent Disk recovered, shortly after europe-west2-b recovery. A small number of remaining instances were fully recovered by 20 Oct 2026, 11:00 US/Pacific (19:00 BST).
**Next Steps:**
Our engineering team is implementing improvements across our database and storage infrastructure to ensure that High Availability instances using Regional Persistent Disks recover more rapidly during unplanned outages.
### Google Kubernetes Engine
**Impact:**
The power loss in europe-west2-b caused total zonal failure, autoscaling stalls, API error spikes, and regional pod unavailability across GKE clusters. Total incident duration for GKE was 7 hours and 34 minutes, starting at 23:02 US/Pacific (07:02 BST), reaching initial mitigation at 05:22 US/Pacific (13:22 BST), and achieving final resolution at 06:37 US/Pacific (14:37 BST).

The scale ups in surviving zones were impacted by available capacity. Autoscaling was slowed down due to increased load and failures of underlying APIs, such as Google Compute Engine (see above).

### Google Cloud Dataflow
**Impact:**
Dataflow mostly behaved as expected for a zonal failure: new batch jobs were automatically routed away from europe-west2-b within about one minute, and all workloads (streaming and batch) recovered with no data loss once power returned. Jobs running in the affected zone also resumed responding to user cancellation requests once the zone came back up.
Additionally, we identified and have now fixed an issue that caused increased streaming job start latency for about two hours. Google engineering is actively working to resolve a zone-selection issue that incorrectly routed a small number of new jobs to the unavailable zone.

A manual rolling restart of messaging infrastructure across all instances brought unavailable Looker instances down to about 15% within about two hours of onset. Subsequently, regional control-plane issues in GKE pushed instance unavailability back to about 35% before settling near 20% for several hours. **Next Steps**:

## Preliminary Incident Report
We recognize that Google Cloud services are critical to your organization, and we sincerely apologize for the disruption this incident may have caused to your business. We are working to address the root cause and prevent this from occurring in the future.
Please note, this information is based on our best knowledge at the time of posting and is subject to change as our investigation continues. A final Incident Report with preventative actions will be posted once our investigation is complete.
If you have experienced impact outside of what is listed below, please reach out to Google Cloud Support using [**https\://cloud.google.com/support**](https://cloud.google.com/support).
## Date/Time of the Issue
Incident Start:19 Oct 2026 23:00 US/Pacific / 20 Oct 2026 07:00 BST
Incident End: 20 Oct 2026 05:10 US/Pacific / 20 Oct 2026 13:10 BST
Duration: 6 hours, 10 minutes
## Summary
On Monday, 19 October 2026 (Tuesday, 20 October BST), multiple Google Cloud Platform services in the europe-west2 region experienced service disruptions, elevated error rates, Application Programming Interface (API) timeouts, and processing latency for a duration of 6 hours and 10 minutes. The disruption was triggered by an electrical power interruption at the datacenter facility hosting availability zone europe-west2-b, which temporarily took physical host servers, network routing hardware, and storage systems offline. This subsequently caused secondary failover and queuing delays across unimpacted regional infrastructure. 
## Preliminary Root Cause
The incident was triggered when a power grid disruption occurred at the datacenter facility hosting availability zone europe-west2-b. To maintain continuous power during the disruption, automatic transfer to facility backup power systems was triggered immediately. The facility load was transferred to the Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) battery banks during the start up sequence of on-site emergency diesel generators. The Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) automation system (both primary and backup PLCs) failed to initiate the logical automatic start/transfer operations of the generators, preventing backup generators from assuming the load. When UPS battery reserves were depleted, physical host servers, network switching fabric, and local storage arrays dedicated to europe-west2-b lost power and went offline.
The sequence of events leading to customer impact was as follows:
* At 22:53 US/Pacific (20 Oct, 06:53 BST), an electrical power disruption occurred at the datacenter facility hosting availability zone europe-west2-b, and a PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) startup fault prevented facility emergency generators from assuming the electrical load. Facility load continued to be supported by UPS battery banks until the batteries were depleted, starting at 23:00 US/Pacific (20 Oct, 07:00 BST).
* When the physical host servers, local storage infrastructure, and network aggregation hardware in europe-west2-b lost power, it caused instances, database replicas, and worker nodes in that zone to become immediately unreachable.
* Regional traffic-routing mechanisms and client applications initiated automated failover toward available infrastructure in adjacent availability zones within the region.
* Cross-zone remote procedure calls from regional service control planes directed to metadata and catalog components in the offline zone encountered timeouts, causing initial job submission stalls and API latency spikes.
* The sudden influx of redirected query executions, high-availability database failovers, and compute workloads saturated available compute slots and processing capacity in other availability zones, creating elevated admission queues, delayed database failover completions, and intermittent 500 and 503 API errors across the region.
Google engineers have begun a full root cause analysis (RCA) and will provide additional information once it is available.
## Remediation
Google engineers were alerted to the disruption via automated monitoring systems and probers at 23:08 US/Pacific on 19 Oct (20 Oct, 07:08 BST), which detected elevated API error ratios, job submission timeouts, and loss of infrastructure reachability in europe-west2-b. Engineering teams immediately mobilized to isolate the affected infrastructure and commence recovery:
* **Traffic Isolation:** Google engineers isolated the offline availability zone (europe-west2-b) by adjusting regional service routing away from the affected infrastructure, preventing cross-zone client requests from timing out against offline endpoints.
* **Workload Reprioritization and Resource Safeguards:** Engineers adjusted scheduler allocations and capacity limits across unimpacted infrastructure to prioritize active customer reservations, reduce resource contention on execution slots, and relieve queue backlogs for regional workloads.
* **Power Grid Restoration:** On-site facility engineers conducted graceful restoration of a stable utility power feed once utility supply was back, within 1 hour. Following this, they focused and completed a reset and tested the emergency backup generator automation controllers to restore facility power.
* **Progressive Infrastructure Re-activation:** Google engineers systematically restarted core Google Cloud infrastructure and services.
* **Controlled Traffic Re-admission:** Once system health and storage integrity were verified, engineers executed gradual, controlled traffic re-admission back to zone europe-west2-b allowing accumulated job backlogs to clear smoothly.
By 05:10 US/Pacific on Tuesday, 20 Oct(13:10 BST), service availability had recovered for the vast majority of customer workloads, and resolution for most of the customers across Google Cloud Platform services in the region was confirmed. Following the recovery of a small tail of remaining isolated workloads, the closure notification for the incident was posted by 07:03 US/Pacific (15:03 BST).
## Description of Impact
Between Monday, 19 Oct 2026, 23:00 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 07:00 BST) and Tuesday, 20 October 2026, 05:10 US/Pacific (13:10 BST), customers utilizing Google Cloud Platform services in the europe-west2 region experienced service disruptions across two consecutive phases, lasting a total duration of 6 hours, 10 minutes.
During the initial phase from 23:00 to 04:29 US/Pacific (07:00 to 12:29 BST) (duration 5 hours, 29 minutes), customers experienced elevated error rates, API timeouts, and processing delays until most Google Cloud Platform services recovered.
Following platform service restoration, some customer workloads running on Compute Engine instances experienced a longer recovery tail. By 04:46 US/Pacific (12:46 BST) new Virtual Machine creation resumed and by 05:10 US/Pacific (13:10 BST) over 99% of Compute Engine Virtual Machines were in a healthy state. Any remaining customers that were experiencing Virtual Machine problems were directed to file a customer support issue as per normal procedure.
While the physical power outage was isolated strictly to datacenter facilities in europe-west2-b, some customers running workloads in unimpacted zones (europe-west2-a and europe-west2-c) or across regional architectures also experienced unexpected impact.
The primary causes were 1\) instantaneous demand surges on unimpacted compute capacity and 2\) synchronous control-plane validation dependencies across zonal boundaries. Affected products included: BigQuery, Looker, Google Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, Regional Persistent Disk, and Cloud SQL. These services experienced unexpected degradation and failover issues driven by sudden compute capacity exhaustion from surging demand, and control-plane API timeouts waiting on validations from the offline zone.
Workloads and resources hosted entirely within europe-west2-b became unreachable. Data storage services with failover capability such as Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Memorystore for Redis, and Cloud Bigtable failed over into nearby unimpacted zones during the europe-west2-b outage. Multi-zonal and regional services that spanned across the europe-west2 region experienced elevated latency, transient API errors (such as HTTP 500 and 503 errors), and task admission queuing as failover traffic concentrated onto unimpacted regional resources and cross-zone calls to offline components timed out. Storage write operations in the region experienced a transient error rate during the initial failover period, and regional query admission queues temporarily peaked before rapidly subsiding as capacity re-balanced.

## Incident Report
### **Summary**
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 (Tuesday, 20 Oct BST), a data center facility that hosts europe-west2-b, experienced an external electrical power disruption. This resulted in service unavailability for workloads located in this zone. As traffic was redirected to alternative cloud regions or unaffected zones within europe-west2 cloud region, these workloads experienced transient latency and elevated errors affecting services across europe-west2. 
The primary impact was mitigated after 6 hours 8 minutes.
### **Root Cause**
**Facility architecture and background:**
The data center facility in the UK region hosts Cloud clusters serving the europe-west2-b zone, which form part of the multi-zonal europe-west2 Cloud region. The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture—meaning the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load—backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC).
Primary utility power is supplied to the facility via two independent feeders (A and B), supplemented by a standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events. The two high-voltage primary feeders terminate at separate primary intake switchboards capable of closed-loop operation if either board is taken offline. Switching between the primary and standby utility providers utilizes open transitions and key interlocks to prevent parallel connections across sources.
Static Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) battery systems provide 5 minutes of autonomous runtime. This bridge power ensures uninterrupted operation while the PLC detects utility undervoltage events, initiates diesel generator startup, synchronizes the generators, and transfers the site load.
Prior to the utility disruption, the facility had been placed in a temporary single-feed (1N) bridged maintenance posture on the primary utility. Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened and key-interlocked (Locked Out Tagged Out) to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026. Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while repairs were conducted on the B feeder pathway.
**Root Cause:**
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 at 22:53 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 06:53 BST), the primary utility provider experienced an outage on primary utility feed A, caused by an external underground cable fault on the utility network outside the data center facility.  
When the primary utility feed A was lost, the facility’s generator plant failed to receive a signal to automatically start and take critical load due to a design voltage-sensing and misconfiguration in the PLCs. The facility's static UPS battery banks carried the critical load as designed until their battery reserves depleted resulting in a complete power loss across data halls.
The investigation of the PLC configuration identified the root cause as a misconfiguration of the PLC logic that did not verify both an undervoltage condition and physical breaker position for both utility feeders. Instead, the PLC undervoltage sensing inputs were wired upstream (line side) of the isolated utility feed B breaker. The PLC was programmed to verify whether voltage was present on the feeder before commanding a generator start. As the utility feed B remained energized upstream, both PLCs sensed live upstream voltage on the disconnected path. As a result, the PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant.;
The onsite facilities team attempted to execute a remote load transfer via the PLC; however, the system inhibited the action. Recognizing that the UPS battery reserves would be exhausted before further remote operations could be resolved, the team transferred the facility load to the standby utility source, restoring the critical load that was lost once batteries depleted during this process.
Once utility power was restored via the standby utility source, and UPS batteries started recharging, the onsite facility teams and OEM vendors reconfigured and validated PLC functionality on both undervoltage and breaker status.
After the power loss was initially detected, Google engineers began work to mitigate failover failures and prepare service recovery. Upon restoration of the utility source, UPS and generator capabilities, they began the process to re-enable services in europe-west2-b.
### Remediation and Prevention
The sequence of events leading to customer impact was as follows:
* **19 Oct 22:53 US/Pacific (20 Oct BST 06:53 BST) -** An electrical power disruption occurred at the data center facility hosting availability zone europe-west2-b, and a PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) startup fault prevented facility emergency generators from assuming the electrical load. Facility load continued to be supported by UPS battery banks until the batteries were depleted.
* **19 Oct 23:00 US/Pacific (20 Oct 07:00 BST)** **Impact start -** As battery backups were exhausted, physical host servers, local storage infrastructure, and network aggregation hardware in availability zone europe-west2-b lost power, causing instances, database replicas, and worker nodes in that zone to become immediately unreachable.
* **19 Oct 23:04 US/Pacific (20 Oct 07:04 BST) -** Google engineers were alerted to the disruption via automated monitoring systems and probers, which detected elevated API error ratios, job submission timeouts, and loss of infrastructure reachability in zone europe-west2-b. Engineering teams immediately mobilized to isolate the affected infrastructure and commence recovery.

Google Compute Engine's zonal resources such as VMs require customers to provision failover or cross-zone recovery resources if needed, and to set up a recovery mechanism that matches their needs.

Storage write operations in the region experienced a transient error rate during the initial failover period, and regional query admission queues temporarily peaked before rapidly subsiding as capacity re-balanced.

This resulted in service unavailability for workloads located in this zone. As traffic was redirected to alternative cloud regions or unaffected zones within europe-west2 cloud region, these workloads experienced transient latency and elevated errors affecting services across europe-west2. 
The primary impact was mitigated after 6 hours 8 minutes.
### **Root Cause**
**Facility architecture and background:**
The data center facility in the UK region hosts Cloud clusters serving the europe-west2-b zone, which form part of the multi-zonal europe-west2 Cloud region. The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture—meaning the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load—backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC).
Primary utility power is supplied to the facility via two independent feeders (A and B), supplemented by a standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events. The two high-voltage primary feeders terminate at separate primary intake switchboards capable of closed-loop operation if either board is taken offline. Switching between the primary and standby utility providers utilizes open transitions and key interlocks to prevent parallel connections across sources.
Static Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) battery systems provide 5 minutes of autonomous runtime. This bridge power ensures uninterrupted operation while the PLC detects utility undervoltage events, initiates diesel generator startup, synchronizes the generators, and transfers the site load.
Prior to the utility disruption, the facility had been placed in a temporary single-feed (1N) bridged maintenance posture on the primary utility. Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened and key-interlocked (Locked Out Tagged Out) to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026. Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while repairs were conducted on the B feeder pathway.
**Root Cause:**
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 at 22:53 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 06:53 BST), the primary utility provider experienced an outage on primary utility feed A, caused by an external underground cable fault on the utility network outside the data center facility.  
When the primary utility feed A was lost, the facility’s generator plant failed to receive a signal to automatically start and take critical load due to a design voltage-sensing and misconfiguration in the PLCs. The facility's static UPS battery banks carried the critical load as designed until their battery reserves depleted resulting in a complete power loss across data halls.
The investigation of the PLC configuration identified the root cause as a misconfiguration of the PLC logic that did not verify both an undervoltage condition and physical breaker position for both utility feeders. Instead, the PLC undervoltage sensing inputs were wired upstream (line side) of the isolated utility feed B breaker. The PLC was programmed to verify whether voltage was present on the feeder before commanding a generator start. As the utility feed B remained energized upstream, both PLCs sensed live upstream voltage on the disconnected path. As a result, the PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant.;
The onsite facilities team attempted to execute a remote load transfer via the PLC; however, the system inhibited the action. Recognizing that the UPS battery reserves would be exhausted before further remote operations could be resolved, the team transferred the facility load to the standby utility source, restoring the critical load that was lost once batteries depleted during this process.
Once utility power was restored via the standby utility source, and UPS batteries started recharging, the onsite facility teams and OEM vendors reconfigured and validated PLC functionality on both undervoltage and breaker status.

fields.title: Disruption with Copilot Cloud services

updates.body: We are investigating reports of impacted performance for some GitHub services.

We are experiencing increased failures and latency on our agent sessions service, including creating and listing sessions. This can impact cloud based agent sessions on web, mobile, VS Code, CLI and the GitHub Copilot app.

We continue to experience failure rates of 1-2% and increased latency on our agent sessions service, including creating and listing sessions. This can impact cloud based agent sessions on web, mobile, VS Code, CLI and the GitHub Copilot app.

We continue to experience failure rates of 1-2% and increased latency on our agent sessions service, including creating and listing sessions. This can impact cloud based agent sessions on web, mobile, VS Code, CLI and the GitHub Copilot app. We are actively applying mitigations and monitoring for recovery.
The degradation has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

On October 29, 2026, between 05:50 UTC and 12:40 UTC, Copilot agent sessions on GitHub.com and in VS Code were degraded. Live session updates often failed to load, and on average 2.14% of requests to the agent sessions service failed, with a peak of 8.61%. For about 10 minutes around 09:20 UTC, up to 40% of requests to list or create agent sessions failed. Copilot Chat on GitHub.com showed degraded agent session features during this time. The issue occurred when a large increase in task-list requests from a client experiment overloaded the cache that supports the agent sessions service. We mitigated the impact by increasing cache capacity, reducing nonessential load on the cache, and disabling the client experiment. We are moving rate limiting to separate infrastructure, reducing client polling, and improving our alerting so we can detect and respond to this type of overload faster.

fields.title: Several GPT models degraded

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded availability for Copilot AI Model Providers

We are experiencing degraded availability for the GPT-5.2, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 Mini, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, and GPT-5.6 Luna models in Copilot products and IDE surfaces. This is due to an issue with an upstream model provider. While we work with them to resolve the issue, we recommend choosing another model or selecting 'Auto' to continue using Copilot.
The degradation affecting Copilot AI Model Providers has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

On July 25, 2026, between 09:07 and 10:04 UTC, the GPT-5.2, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 Mini, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-5.6 Luna models experienced degraded availability in GitHub Copilot products and IDE surfaces. Requests to these models had an average failure rate of 5.6%. Other Copilot models remained available as alternatives.

The degradation was caused by an issue with an upstream model provider. Success rates returned to normal after the upstream issue was mitigated, and we continued monitoring before resolving the incident. We are working on improving the automated failover for the affected models to prevent similar incidents in the future.

fields.title: Incident with Actions

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded performance for Actions

We’re investigating an issue causing delays when assigning GitHub-hosted runners to Actions jobs. Some workflows may take longer to start across runner configurations. Our teams are working to mitigate the issue, and we’ll provide an update as we learn more.

We’re still investigating delays in assigning GitHub-hosted runners, affecting workflow start times across multiple runner configurations. Our teams are working to mitigate the impact; we’ll share another update as we learn more.

We’re continuing to investigate job failures and delays affecting GitHub-hosted runner assignment and workflow start times. Our teams are actively working to mitigate the impact and will provide another update as we learn more.
Actions is experiencing degraded availability. We are continuing to investigate.

In addition to ongoing issues with Actions and Hosted Runners, some customers are also unable to access repository list, licensing and billing pages within their GitHub accounts. We continue to investigate and are working on mitigation.
Pages is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.
Actions is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.

We have applied mitigations to address GitHub Actions failures. Queued jobs are clearing, new jobs are not delayed, and we expect full runner recovery shortly. We continue to monitor for full recovery and are working to mitigate ongoing issues affecting other services, including access to repository lists, licensing, and billing pages.
Actions is operating normally.
Pages is operating normally.

On October 5, 2026, between 18:48 and 22:49 UTC, GitHub Actions and Hosted Runners experienced degraded performance. Over the full incident, 14.3% of workflow runs using GitHub-hosted runners and 26.5% of individual GitHub-hosted jobs did not start within five minutes.


During the roughly 90-minute period of highest impact, 47.0% of workflow runs using GitHub-hosted runners failed and 71.9% of GitHub-hosted jobs did not start within five minutes, while existing Pages sites continued to serve normally. A portion of customers also encountered intermittent errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features. Self-hosted runners were not affected.


The incident was caused by a partial networking failure that disrupted connectivity between one of our on-premises datacenter regions and a subset of cloud-hosted regional database and storage services.


We mitigated the incident by shifting database and storage traffic to healthy regions and endpoints and increasing capacity for affected compute services. GitHub Actions and Hosted Runners recovered by 21:54 UTC, and all affected services recovered by 22:49 UTC.


We are partnering with our cloud provider to understand the network failure and identify improvements to network-path resilience, detection, and recovery for similar incidents.

fields.title: Worker's Observarbility Issues

updates.body: Cloudflare is aware, and investigating reports where a subset of customers are not seeing logs in the Workers Observability dashboard after deploying a new version of a Worker. Affected Workers continue to run and serve traffic normally. Metrics remain available.

We have identified the root cause and reverted the impacted change. However, for the fix to apply to existing Workers utilizing Gradual Deployments, affected Workers must have their deployment traffic percentages adjusted or redeployed. 

As a workaround, if you are currently impacted, you can immediately resolve the issue for your service by modifying the traffic weights of your Gradual Deployment (for example, shifting your active deployment weights from 50%/50% to 40%/60%, or redeploying your Worker).

We are actively working on an automated fix for all remaining affected customers and will provide another update once resolved.
This incident has been resolved.

fields.title: Incident with several GitHub Services

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded availability for API Requests, Issues, Pages and Pull Requests
Actions is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.

We're seeing increased database replication delays on collab which is causing increased error rates in authorization endpoints and follow-on increased error rates across the system - we are investigating
We have reduced load on this cluster with internal load-shedding and are seeing signs of recovery but continue to monitor
Pull Requests is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.

On September 13, 2026, between 08:43 and 10:44 UTC, GitHub experienced degraded availability across approximately 28 services, including Issues, Pull Requests, Actions, Codespaces, Pages, Notifications, Code Scanning, Git LFS, and new account signup. At peak, 8.8% of requests to create GitHub App installation access tokens failed. Token issuance for Actions workflows was also affected, impacting approximately 4% of workflows during the incident time frame. Creating issues through the web interface failed for about 96% of attempts, and signup failures were above 90%.

The cause was an internal data-cleanup job that began writing to a shared database cluster at 07:33 UTC. That cluster stores permission data read on nearly every authenticated request. The safeguard that was pacing the background job watched only one health signal — how far the database replicas were lagging — and that signal stayed low the whole time. It did not account for the load building on the primary itself, so the job kept writing while the primary quietly ran toward its limit.

When the primary ran out of available connections, requests that needed it could not complete. First, there was no quick timeout on these database calls, so request handlers waited on the stalled database instead of failing fast, and the shared request-handling capacity degraded into site-wide errors. Second, a retry loop around token creation kept re-sending the writes that were already failing, which held the database saturated rather than letting it recover.

Monitoring declared the incident at 08:50 UTC, but due to the broad impact and amplification from token creation, it took time to identify the source of the load. First responders mitigated by shedding internal load and pausing the job, and all services recovered by 10:44 UTC.

To prevent recurrence, we are rate-limiting background jobs against shared, customer-serving databases by default, and adding automatic pausing and paging on primary-server load rather than replication lag alone. We are also surfacing running background work directly alongside database health signals so responders can see and pause it without leaving those dashboards, bounding retries in the token-issuing path, and adding request-level timeouts so one unhealthy database cannot consume shared web server capacity. In addition, we are breaking apart this database cluster to remove the single point of failure. We will be moving various service-specific data, including the authorization data, out of this shared cluster in the next two weeks.

fields.title: Incident with Actions

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded performance for Actions
The degradation affecting Actions has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

We identified an issue causing delays in GitHub Actions run starts. Some users may have experienced longer than expected wait times when triggering workflow runs. We have applied mitigations and have recovered. Our team continues to monitor and investigate the root cause.

On July 25, 2026, GitHub Actions experienced two related periods of degradation that caused some workflow runs to be delayed by more than 5 minutes or end with infrastructure failures.

First period (08:45 – 09:13 UTC): During planned maintenance on a critical-path Redis cluster for Actions, one participating region was left in a degraded state. Separately, an independent capacity operation temporarily removed another region from the cluster and redirected its traffic to the degraded region. This created cross-region inconsistencies in job-assignment state, causing workflow runs to be delayed, exhaust retries, or fail outright. At peak, about 7% of runs were delayed by more than 5 minutes, and 25% of runs failed with an infrastructure error during the course of the incident. We mitigated the incident at 09:13 UTC by returning traffic to its normal distribution.

Second period (12:08 – 12:48 UTC): As part of mitigating the first incident, traffic was returned to the regional instance that was still undergoing its capacity increase. Multiple Redis nodes in the scaling region experienced failures, increasing traffic to healthy nodes and causing connection limits to be reached on many nodes. At peak, 30% of runs were delayed by more than 5 minutes, and 60% of runs failed with an infrastructure error during the course of the incident. We mitigated the incident at 12:48 UTC by redirecting workflow traffic away from the scaling region.

We are adding stronger regional health and capacity checks before maintenance and requiring a stable observation period before restoring traffic. We are also improving automated connection resiliency, and partnering with our platform dependency to automatically detect and remediate unhealthy cluster members and shard imbalance. More generally, we already had work underway to improve the resiliency and scale of this piece of Actions infrastructure.

fields.title: Free Plan Customers Are Experiencing Message Failures

updates.body:
We're aware that some customers on our free plan are experiencing message-sending limit blocks in an unusual spike pattern, which is preventing them from sending messages. We're investigating why this message limit was triggered unexpectedly for some teams. If you're affected, you may be temporarily unable to send messages until this is resolved.
We'll provide an update in 30 minutes or sooner if additional information becomes available.

We identified that a third-party app is stuck in a loop that has triggered billions of messages. This is causing free plan users to exceed messaging limits.
We apologize for the inconvenience and will provide another update as soon as we have more details to share.

A feature toggle ramp-up caused an app integration to repeatedly post messages in a processing loop. This pushed free plan customers over the message volume threshold, triggering the sending block. We're working to restore access and are actively working on remediation options for impacted Workspaces.
We apologize for the inconvenience and will provide another update as soon as we have more details to share.

We’ve identified a potential fix for this issue and we’re working on getting this out to users as quickly as possible. We’ll be back once we have another update to share.
Thank you for your continued patience as we work towards a solution.

Deployment of the fix is underway to restore access for impacted free plan workspaces, and we are actively monitoring the environment. More information will follow as we progress through this stage of remediation.

A messaging integration briefly caused some free-plan workspaces to exceed their daily messaging limit, blocking them from sending messages. We took action to lift the sending block for all affected free-plan workspaces, and have confirmed messaging is now restored. We apologize for how this incident affected you and your business. We will undertake a full investigation of the incident, establishing the technical trigger, the underlying cause, and preventive action to avoid a repeat in the future.

fields.title: Incident with Actions

updates.body: We are investigating reports of impacted performance for some GitHub services.

On August 18, 2026, between 05:02 UTC and 11:30 UTC, customers were unable to run jobs on Actions Larger Runners and were unable to view or manage Actions Runners and Runner Groups through the GitHub UI and API.

These issues were caused by failures in backend requests resolving essential metadata for starting Larger Runner workflow runs and for reading runner and runner group data. The failures were caused by an expired authentication certificate unique to this service. The certificate had been rotated in KeyVault, but a step to enable use at runtime had been paused to prevent recurrence of previous incidents that had been triggered by this operation.

We mitigated the issues by completing the enablement of the new certificate in the backend system. We have added additional monitoring to this and other certificates. The relevant service is also in the process of being replaced as part of our availability and scale work, bringing this authentication path and secret management in line with patterns across all GitHub services.

fields.title: Elevated Launch Failures

updates.body: We are experiencing elevated launch failures in the US-WEST-2 Region.

We are experiencing elevated launch failures in the US-WEST-2 Region caused by an issue with the EBS service. Services that depend on EBS or EC2 will experience failure rates of their own. We are working to mitigate the issues. We will provide you with another update by 4:00 PM PST or sooner if new information becomes available.

We can confirm EC2 instance launch failures affecting all AZs (usw2-az1, usw2-az2, usw2-az3, usw2-az4) in the US-WEST-2 Region. We have identified the issue to be caused by a  subsystem that supports EBS Volumes required during instance launch. Services that instantiate new instances, such as cross-region data copy for DataSync, within the US-WEST-2 Region as either the source or destination are also affected. We recommend that customers do not mutate running instances at this time that would result in the replacement or creation of a new EC2 instance in the Region. Running EC2 instances and already created EBS volumes continue to operate as normal. 

We are seeing early signs of recovery, and continue to take steps to restore launches within the Region. We will update this post by 5:30 PM PST or earlier if we have new information to share.

Between 2:35 PM and 4:21 PM PST, we experienced elevated EC2 instance launch failures affecting all AZs (usw2-az1, usw2-az2, usw2-az3, usw2-az4) in the US-WEST-2 Region. EC2 Instance Launches, AWS services that instantiated new instances, as well as services such as DataSync or AWS Backup which require new instances to support data transfers to or from the US-WEST-2 Region were affected. Our engineers were automatically engaged and immediately began investigating the root cause. We identified the issue to be caused by a subsystem that supports EBS Volumes required during instance launch. We began remediation of that issue at 3:20 PM, and completed full recovery at 4:21 PM. We recommend customers retry requests that failed during this time. Running EC2 instances and already created EBS volumes were not impacted and continued to operate as normal. The issue has been resolved and all AWS services are now operating normally.

Between July 19, 2026, at 23:05 UTC and July 20, 2026, at 03:55 UTC, Actions self-hosted and larger runners were unable to connect to GitHub. During this period, Actions jobs were delayed or failed when trying to acquire a runner. Jobs using standard and Mac hosted runners were not affected. Reconnection traffic from affected runners also increased load on GitHub APIs, resulting in 3-4 seconds of additional average request latency and elevated 5xx error rates.

The incident was caused by a certificate lifecycle management failure in a subset of internal services, resulting in an SSL certificate expiration that disrupted runner connectivity. We restored service by rotating the affected certificate. Recovery began at 02:45 UTC. By 03:55 UTC, queued workflow backlog had been processed and workflow delay rates returned to normal.

To prevent recurrence, we are strengthening certificate renewal automation, adding fallback expiry monitoring and alerting, and improving circuit-breaker protections during runner API disruptions to reduce the risk of cascading impact to other APIs.

On October 21, 2026, between 13:22 UTC and 19:22 UTC, several GitHub services were delayed due to degradation of our internal event streaming platform.

Pull request updates, push webhooks, and push-triggered Actions workflows were delayed by up to 33 minutes until 15:36 UTC. Actions status updates were delayed by up to 33 minutes until 16:16 UTC, holding up some merges and deployments that wait on checks. Webhook deliveries and live updates were delayed by up to 25 minutes until 16:52 UTC. Audit log events were delayed by up to two hours.

This was due to servers in the platform running out of memory caused by client reconnections without sufficient retry backoff. We mitigated the incident by moving the busiest workloads to less-loaded servers and adding capacity.

We have since added reconnection backoff and added server capacity. We are building a solution for auto-rebalancing connections across servers, and splitting the platform into smaller, isolated clusters to reduce blast radius and time to mitigation of issues like this one in the future.

updates.body:
Cloudflare identified an issue that delayed a small subset of single file cache purge requests between 19:21 and 20:21 UTC on November 22, 2026. Affected requests were submitted through Cloudflare data centers in parts of Europe, the Middle East and Africa. For these requests, cached content in other Cloudflare data centers worldwide could remain stale for up to approximately 60 minutes before the purge completed. 

All delayed purges have since completed, and this incident has been resolved.
