fields.title: Incident with Webhooks

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded performance for Webhooks

Between 15:17 and 15:27 UTC, an ongoing deployment had an unintended side effect where webhook delivery states were not persisted in all cases, even when deliveries were accepted and processed. Customers may notice missing webhook deliveries in the UI, and these deliveries will not be retryable.

Impact resolved automatically once the deployment completed.
The degradation affecting Webhooks has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

On July 14, 2026, between 15:17 and 15:37 UTC, a rollout to GitHub's internal webhook delivery pipeline caused a subset of webhook delivery records to not be written to our webhook deliveries store after being processed and delivered successfully. Affected deliveries would be missing from the webhook delivery UI and API and won’t be available for redelivery.

The root cause was an uncoordinated rollout: a change to how delivery records are handed off between pipeline components was deployed before the upstream components producing those records were updated to match. While the rollout was in progress, affected records were silently skipped rather than persisted, with no automatic retry. The impact ended as soon as the rollout was completed.

About 2.4M delivery records were skipped (approximately 4% of the 20-minute impact window, 0.04% of a typical 24-hour period). Importantly, 95% of these skipped deliveries reached customer endpoints successfully, only the record of the delivery is missing. Of the ~5% that failed to reach customer endpoints, only ~1.4% (5,463) map to webhooks that retried their deliveries in the past 28 days.

To prevent recurrence, we are improving our automated detection of unsafe schema changes and tightening rollout coordination for changes that span multiple components in the pipeline.

fields.title: Increased task-related errors for Copilot Mission Control

updates.body: We are investigating reports of impacted performance for some GitHub services.
Copilot Mission Control is experiencing increased error rates (approx 2.5%) in listing and creating tasks due to upstream database throttling. We are investigating two potential mitigations.
We've identified the issue with a specific client version and are deploying a mitigation. We are already seeing partial recovery.
We're continuing to see recovery as rollout continues
The degradation has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

On November 4, 2026, between approximately 03:40 UTC and 10:01 UTC, some Copilot agent users experienced errors listing and creating agent tasks. On average, 1.22% of requests were failed, with a peak of 2.68% over a ten-minute interval.

The issue occurred when increased task-list traffic and expensive queries exhausted shared database capacity. We mitigated the broader impact by disabling a client experiment and temporarily restricting task-list requests from the affected client. Task-list requests remained restricted after the wider service recovered; we removed the blanket restriction on November 6 and continued a gradual rollout.

We’ve since improved task-list queries, moved rate limiting to separate infrastructure and added capacity monitoring. We’re continuing to reduce unnecessary client requests and validate capacity before expanding the rollout to reduce the chance of recurrence.

fields.title: Increased API Error Rates

updates.body: Starting at 2:12 PM PDT, we began experiencing increased API error rates for STS and Sign In when using SAML in the US-WEST-2 Region. Our engineering team was automatically engaged at 2:19 PM to begin investigating the root cause. There is no work around available at this time. We will provide another update by 3:30 PM PDT.
We are seeing early signs of recovery and continue to monitor for full recovery. We will provide another update at 4:15 PM, or sooner if we have additional information to share.

We continue to see recovery holding steady for the STS AssumeRoleWithSAML and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity APIs in the US-WEST-2 Region. Error rates are now back to pre-event levels, and we continue actively monitoring to confirm full recovery. We will provide another update by 5:15 PM or earlier.

Between 2:12 PM and 3:18 PM PDT, we experienced increased API error rates affecting the STS AssumeRoleWithSAML  and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity APIs in the US-WEST-2 Region. The root cause was determined to be due to an issue with an STS subsystem responsible for communicating with external identity providers. Other AWS Services that rely on these identity federation protocols were also affected. At 3:18 PM, we observed signs of recovery and continued to monitor to ensure stability and full recovery. The issue is resolved and the service is operating normally at this time.

fields.title: Multiple Services Availability

updates.body:
Between Aug 6, 06:42 UTC and 09:08 UTC, customers experienced failures with write operations across multiple DigitalOcean services, including Managed Databases, DOKS, Cloud Firewalls, DNS, Spaces, Block Storage Volumes, and event processing.

Customers attempting to update Cloud Firewall rules, modify DNS records, manage object storage operations, provision or scale DOKS clusters and node pools, and make other infrastructure configuration changes experienced failures. These operations returned errors, preventing customers from managing their resources. Additionally, event processing was delayed or failed during this window, which may have impacted the timeliness of resource status updates and notifications.

The services have recovered and are now operating normally. Customers should no longer experience issues with write operations, configuration changes, or event processing.

We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused. If you continue to experience issues with any of these services, please don't hesitate to open a support ticket. Our team will be happy to assist you.

fields.title: Increased wait time for Machine and Remote Docker jobs

updates.body: Some users might see increased wait times for Machine and Remote Docker jobs due to increased usage. Wait times right now are just under 7 mins. Our team is investigating and we'll post another update shortly. We appreciate your patience.
Our team has applied a fix and we're starting to see wait times recover. We're keeping an eye on this as it continues to rollout and we'll update again shortly. We thank you again for your patience.
Wait times have returned to normal for Machine and Remote Docker. We appreciate your patience as we worked through this.

## Summary

From 13:55 to 15:07 UTC on November 3, customers running Linux machine jobs and Remote Docker saw increased wait times for their jobs to start, and the delays were longest from 14:16 to 14:41. Some Docker jobs also saw increased wait times.

The incident was caused by our usage reaching the vCPU limit on our cloud provider account in our main cloud region. Machine and Docker jobs share this limit, and the additional Docker capacity we have run since the [October 21 incident](https://discuss.circleci.com/t/post-incident-report-oct-21-2026-increased-wait-times-for-gen-2-docker-jobs/54940) brought our usage to the limit as demand increased. Machine jobs did not move to our backup regions because our system did not treat reaching this limit the same way as a shortage of cloud instances.

In response, our engineering team reconfigured machine jobs to balance across all of our regions instead of relying on backup regions, and reduced Docker capacity to make room under the limit. By 14:46, wait times had improved, and by 15:07, machine wait times had fully recovered.

After we resolved the incident, our cloud provider doubled the vCPU limit in our main region. We have also restored the Docker capacity we reduced during the incident.

The original status page can be found here: [Increased wait time for Machine and Remote Docker jobs](https://status.circleci.com/incidents/qqh50c0z6mn3).

## Background

Machine jobs need a dedicated virtual machine, so when CircleCI runs a machine job, we create a fresh virtual machine for that job and delete it when the job ends. Remote Docker runs on these same virtual machines. Docker jobs run on shared cloud instances, and each instance can run multiple isolated jobs.

Our cloud provider sets a vCPU limit for each region, which caps the total computing capacity our account can run there. Machine and Docker jobs run in the same account, so they count against the same vCPU limit. When our usage reaches that limit, the cloud provider rejects requests for new cloud instances until existing ones shut down.

Machine jobs normally run in our main region, with other cloud regions available as backups. If the cloud provider cannot supply the instance types we need in our main region, our system sends new work to a backup region.

Following the October 21 incident, we increased the minimum fleet size for our Docker clusters during weekday peak hours, so that capacity is in place before demand arrives. That capacity counts against the same vCPU limit as machine jobs.

## What Happened

_\(All times UTC\)_

Starting at 13:55 on November 3, Linux machine jobs saw increased wait times because our usage in our main region had reached our vCPU limit, and our cloud provider was rejecting requests for new virtual machines. We had not noticed that our alert for this limit was no longer receiving data, so it did not warn us as our usage approached the limit.

At 13:55, our engineering team was alerted to errors launching new virtual machines and began investigating. By 14:06, 40% of Linux machine jobs waited more than 3 minutes to start. By 14:08, we had confirmed the cause and requested a higher limit from our cloud provider.

Our backup regions had capacity available under their own limits, but machine jobs did not move there because our system did not treat reaching our vCPU limit the same way as a shortage of cloud instances. From 14:16 to 14:41, most Linux machine jobs waited 5-9 minutes to start, and some waited more than 20 minutes.

At 14:34, our engineering team reconfigured machine jobs to balance new work across all of our regions, rather than only using backup regions when our main region runs short. The change took effect at 14:40, and at the same time we reduced the minimum fleet size for our Docker clusters to make room under the limit.

By 14:46, wait times had improved, and nearly all Linux machine jobs started within 3 minutes. Delays of 1-3 minutes for some jobs continued until 15:07. We resolved the incident at 15:08.

Docker jobs also saw increased wait times during the incident. Up to 7% of Docker jobs waited longer than usual to start, and that share rose to 19% between 14:39 and 14:43. Docker wait times returned to normal by 15:13.

## Future Prevention and Process Improvement

**We raised our vCPU limit.** Our cloud provider doubled the vCPU limit in our main region, and we have requested the same increase in our other US regions. We have also requested higher limits for related storage and networking resources. Capacity we reserve in advance counts against the limit whether or not jobs are using it, so we are moving some of our reserved capacity out of our main region.

**We are changing how machine jobs handle the vCPU limit.** We are updating our system to treat reaching a vCPU limit the same way as a shortage of cloud instances, so new work will move to a backup region.

**We are separating machine and Docker capacity.** We are moving machine jobs into their own cloud provider account, so Docker capacity will no longer use up the vCPU limit that machine jobs depend on.

**We are fixing our alerts for cloud provider limits.** We are restoring the data our vCPU limit alert depends on and adding alerts for our other limits, so our engineering team will be warned before usage reaches them. If any of these alerts stops receiving data, our engineering team will be alerted, so a gap like this one does not go unnoticed again.

## Conclusion

Customer experience is our top priority, and we commit to continually improving the reliability of our systems to match the trust that our customers place in us. We thank our customers for their patience while our team worked to resolve this incident.

Please reach out to our support team with any questions or concerns.

If any of these alerts stops receiving data, our engineering team will be alerted, so a gap like this one does not go unnoticed again.

## Conclusion

Customer experience is our top priority, and we commit to continually improving the reliability of our systems to match the trust that our customers place in us. We thank our customers for their patience while our team worked to resolve this incident.

Please reach out to our support team with any questions or concerns.

fields.title: Incident With Webhooks

updates.body:
On June 17, 2026, between 11:35 UTC and 19:20 UTC, the Webhooks service was degraded and delivered webhook payloads with missing installation information. On average, 11.3% of webhook deliveries were impacted. Customers relying on the installation field for authentication or routing were unable to process affected webhooks. A smaller subset of deliveries for the security_advisory event (0.04%) were delivered successfully but were not recorded for redelivery. This was due to a defect in a new delivery code path that failed to include installation data in webhook payloads.

We mitigated the incident by disabling the feature flag controlling the new code path.

We are working to improve our automated validation of webhook payloads, and introduce automated alerting for webhook payload regressions to reduce our time to detection and mitigation of issues like this one in the future.

The following events were affected: branch_protection_configuration, code_scanning_alert, commit_comment, custom_property, custom_property_values, dependabot_alert, deploy_key, deployment_protection_rule, deployment_review, dismissal_request_code_scanning, dismissal_request_secret_scanning, installation_target, member, membership, merge_queue_entry, org_block, organization, projects_v2, projects_v2_item, pull_request_review_thread, repository_ruleset, secret_scanning_alert, secret_scanning_alert_location, secret_scanning_scan, security_and_analysis, star, sub_issues, team, team_add, workflow_job.

updates.body:

This is related to an ongoing incident affecting GitHub. You can follow GitHub's status at https://www.githubstatus.com/incidents/gxycch3076xk. Our engineers are actively investigating. 

We will provide another update as soon as we have more information to share.

We are continuing to see high failure rates from GitHub APIs which are impacting login and workflow processing.

We will continue to monitor the GitHub API for recovery.

What's happening
The upstream incident affecting GitHub has been mitigated and is now being monitored on GitHub's side. You can follow GitHub's status at https://www.githubstatus.com/.

What can you expect
Access to the CircleCI web app, sign-in, and pipeline and workflow processing are returning to normal. You may still see intermittent errors or delayed scheduled pipelines and workflows as systems stabilize. Thank you for your patience while we monitor for full recovery.

We thank you for your patience.

fields.title: Disruption with Copilot for access to some models

updates.body: We are investigating reports of impacted performance for some GitHub services.

We are currently investigating reports of some Copilot users experiencing issues accessing certain models. Affected users may see errors or degraded functionality when attempting to use specific models. We are actively working on a fix and will provide updates as we have more information.
The degradation has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.
The issue has been mitigated across all affected environments. We are currently deploying on a fix to prevent reoccurrence. We will provide another update once the fix has been deployed.
We have deployed and validated the fix to prevent immediate reoccurrence. We will be performing additional work to limit these kinds of failures in the future.

On August 10, 2026, between 19:48 UTC and 20:49 UTC, GitHub Copilot users saw an incomplete list of available models. During this window, the service could return as few as one model instead of the full catalog. Requests that tried to use a model missing from that shortened list failed with a "model not found" error. Copilot requests that used an available model were not affected. This did not affect customers on data-residency (Proxima) environments.

The issue was caused by a change to how model data was published, which our systems could not read back correctly and fell back to a limited default list.

We mitigated the incident by 20:49 UTC and deployed a fix to prevent immediate recurrence by 21:50 UTC. We are adding validation and retry safeguards so that model data is verified before it is served.

We apologize for the disruption.

On November 8, 2026, between 08:43 and 12:29 UTC, unauthenticated requests to github.com and the GitHub REST API experienced elevated error rates. During this period, 11.3% of unauthenticated requests and 46.1% of release asset download requests failed. Authenticated requests were largely unaffected.

Initial errors occurred in a backend service handling unauthenticated web traffic. A subsequent traffic spike caused high CPU utilization on servers in our caching layer. Some servers remained unhealthy after the spike ended, prolonging the disruption. We restored service by restarting caching software and rebooting affected servers.

We are improving monitoring to detect these failures sooner, investigating why affected servers did not recover automatically, and reviewing caching behavior to better protect backend services during failures.

Until mitigation at 10:37 UTC, an average of 26% of webhook deliveries were delayed, peaking at 30%, and the backlog cleared by 11:40 UTC. Some deliveries were delayed by up to 3.5 hours, and delays for a small share began as early as 01:00 UTC. Actions skips events older than 30 minutes, so some workflow runs did not start.

The incident was caused by a degraded host that had slowed one of the cluster's Kafka brokers since November 7. The broker stopped reporting the metrics our alerts rely on, so we did not identify it until it stalled the cluster on November 9.

We mitigated the incident by removing the broker from service. We have since added an alert that pages us within 30 minutes when a host slows a broker this way, so we can remove the broker before it affects customers.

updates.body:

Thank you for your patience throughout this incident. If you continue to experience any issues, please reach out to Support from within your account

## 1. What happened

Between 16:56 UTC and 23:09 UTC on August 24, 2026, customers using DigitalOcean’s Cloud Control Panel, Public API, and dependent product management systems experienced elevated request error rates, peaking at 25%, in two distinct windows totaling 3.5 hours of active degradation within a 6-hour span. Running Droplets, network routing, and block storage \(Volumes\) remained fully functional and unaffected throughout the event. No customer data loss occurred.

The event was initiated during a planned infrastructure migration of the database layer supporting identity, authentication, and authorization services. The migration introduced increased execution latency for a critical authorization query. In response to the elevated query latency, multiple upstream services initiated automated hedged retries. This secondary request amplification led to queue buildup in excess of the authentication service pool's processing throughput, resulting in cascading request timeouts across the authorization path.

To mitigate the initial degradation, engineering teams rerouted authorization traffic onto a single healthy processing path and temporarily disabled hedging for primary callers, successfully restoring service availability. However, upon returning traffic to the standard multipath routing configuration, lingering query latency combined with retry behavior from unhedged callers caused recurrent queue saturation, leading to the second window of degradation.

## 2. Impact

* Active customer accounts \(<2%\) experienced one or more API or Control Panel request failures during the event windows.
* Aggregate failure rates across both impact windows averaged approximately 10% of authenticated requests, with a peak error rate of 25% during the second window.
* Affected management control planes included the Cloud Control Panel, Public API, Kubernetes cluster authentication, Container Registry, and Serverless / AI Inference endpoints.
* Data plane components—including active Droplets, network routing, and block storage volumes—maintained 100% availability, as established connections do not depend on the affected authorization control path. There was zero data loss.

## 3. Current state

All impacted control plane services have been restored to nominal operational capacity. The database infrastructure migration has been completed. Remediation controls have been validated to ensure system stability against similar query latency scenarios.

## 4. Preventing recurrence

To prevent future occurrences and enhance systemic resilience, DigitalOcean has implemented the following technical enhancements:

1. Automated Request Throttling and Circuit Breaking:

Deployed automated circuit breakers across upstream services to detect downstream dependency degradation and automatically suppress hedged/retry amplification. Completed a broad architecture audit to ensure retry suppression and circuit breaking are uniformly enforced across all control plane services.

1. Queue Management and Load Shedding:

Implemented fast-fail load-shedding mechanisms to prevent request queue saturation during dependency slowness, accompanied by proactive telemetry alerts to identify queue backing prior to customer impact.

1. Graceful Service Degradation:

Configured critical authorization components to operate in degraded execution modes utilizing asynchronous, eventually-consistent data replicas during primary database latency events.

## 5. Timeline

| **Time UTC** | **Event** |
| --- | --- |
| 16:56 | A specific authorization query began running significantly slower than its historical baseline. |
| 16:58 | Automated monitoring detected abnormal error rates and latency; detected within 5 minutes of impact starting. |
| 17:05–18:52 | Operators tuned retry configuration and consolidated requests to a healthy service instance \(first unavailability window closed\). |
| 21:30 | Shifting traffic back to the production pattern caused the same saturation problem \(second unavailability window begins\). |
| 21:30–23:09 | Teams disabled the retry/amplification behavior across the remaining affected services and added additional read capacity for the slow query. Service was restored to a stable state. |

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded availability for Pages

We’re investigating issues impacting multiple GitHub products including Actions, Pages, and Copilot products.
Copilot is experiencing degraded availability. We are continuing to investigate.
The degradation affecting Actions, Copilot, Pages and Webhooks has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.
We’re seeing recovery across all services and continuing to monitor. The backlog of Actions jobs are being processed. We’ll update when we see full recovery.
The backlog of Actions jobs has been fully processed. We’re observing full recovery across all impacted services.

On November 11, 2026, from 20:05 to 21:02 UTC, customers experienced delayed or failed Actions workflow starts, webhook errors and delivery delays, slower GitHub Apps API requests, and reduced availability of Copilot features, including Code Review. GitHub Pages builds were also delayed.

Nearly all GitHub Actions runs triggered between 20:18 and 20:55 UTC were delayed or failed, leaving approximately 3.4 million partially created runs that are being canceled. No GitHub Pages deployments completed during the incident. In the Central US data residency stamp, between 20:06 and 20:50 UTC, about 63% of webhook API requests failed and 27% of deliveries were not recorded; those deliveries reached their destinations but remain unavailable to view or redeliver. Between approximately 20:20 and 21:00 UTC, Copilot code review on github.com completed 87% fewer reviews than normal and some other Copilot features were also unavailable.

The disruption was caused by an Azure Cosmos DB regional outage affecting database accounts used by these services. Per Cosmos’s RCA, a configuration change to the Central US gateways exposed a latent race condition under a specific high-load traffic pattern, causing gateway crashes and health-probe failures. Cosmos mitigated by rolling back the change. Service health recovered around 21:02 UTC, and the queued Actions backlog finished processing by 21:21 UTC.

Our follow-up work focuses on validating regional database failover across affected services and developing tested recovery procedures. We are also improving recovery tools to quickly clear stuck Actions checks and runs after incidents so they do not remain uncancelable or block pull request merges.

fields.title: Issues with Workers VPC hostname route resolution on 2026-09-11

updates.body:
An issue prevented Workers VPC from correctly resolving hostname routes for a small subset of accounts between 06:22 and 09:38 UTC on Friday, September 11th, 2026. This problem has been fully resolved, and all services are operating normally.

During this timeframe, affected accounts may have experienced connection failures, timeouts, or routing errors when Workers VPC attempted to fetch requests via hostname routes.

The issue was strictly limited to hostname route resolution within Workers VPC for the impacted accounts; direct IP-based and public routing, standard Workers executions, and all other services were not affected.

Our engineering team identified and deployed a fix for the root cause, and we are continuing to monitor service metrics to ensure stability. We sincerely apologize for any disruption this may have caused.

On October 22, 2026, from 13:05 to 15:20 UTC, our event streaming platform was degraded resulting in elevated job processing latency spikes of 19-35 seconds and elevated job processing times of 4m – this resulted in delayed Actions workflow and step results (up to 13m), notifications (20m) and repository push events (12m). Recovery for repositories began at 14:32, with Actions recovery beginning at 14:59. The issue reoccurred at 16:26 again impacting Actions runs, repo push events, and notifications. Recovery began at 17:16 and completed at 2:07.

The incident was caused by a significant increase in load coupled with client connection storms during a deployment overloading our Kafka event streaming brokers.

To prevent future recurrence, we have expanded the affected cluster, shifted traffic to less loaded clusters, and implemented tunable client reconnect backoff.

fields.title: Degradation with Webhooks, Pull Requests and Actions

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded performance for Actions, Pull Requests and Webhooks
Actions is experiencing degraded availability. We are continuing to investigate.
Issues is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.
The degradation affecting Actions, Issues, Pull Requests and Webhooks has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

We identified an issue that caused degradation across multiple services including Webhooks, Pull Requests, Actions, and Issues. Customers may have experienced delays or failures with these services. We have applied mitigations and affected services have recovered.

On June 25, 2026, between 17:33 UTC and 17:55 UTC, our background job service experienced degradation which increased delays to pull requests, repository pushes, Actions workflows, and Webhooks, with delays peaking at 7m. The issue was caused by underlying hypervisor issues and an incoming traffic spike, causing service timeouts which led to a connection storm and continual rebalances.

The issue was mitigated by replacing the problem node at 17:49, after which all services saw recovery by 18:07.

fields.title: Delay in data appearing in UI and API

updates.body: There is a delay in our data infrastructure causing delays before build data and some notifications become visible. We are working on a mitigation.

What's impacted: 
Customers triggering pipelines, and customers relying on outbound webhooks and email and Slack notifications.

What can you expect
Since 11:15 UTC:
 - Pipelines are still being created while this is ongoing but not yet processed, so retriggering may result in duplicate pipelines.
 - Outbound webhooks and transactional notifications (Slack and email) are not being sent.
 - Pipeline statuses may not be visible. 
 - Usage charge data on the Project Usage page will be stale. 

Thank you for your patience while our engineers work to resolve this.

Next update: 
We will provide another update by 13:30 UTC.

Between 11:15 UTC and about 13:00 UTC, pipelines were created but not processed, and outbound webhooks and transactional notifications (Slack and email) were not sent.

What's impacted:
Customers triggering pipelines, and customers relying on outbound webhooks and email and Slack notifications.

What can you expect:
- Since about 13:00 UTC, pipelines are being processed again and jobs are starting.

Between 11:15 UTC and 23:47 UTC on October 9, customers experienced delays and failures across pipelines, workflows and jobs, along with delays in the CircleCI UI, API and notifications.

From 11:15 to about 13:00 UTC, pipelines were created but not processed, and outbound webhooks and Slack and email notifications were not sent. From about 13:00 to 14:40 UTC, workflows and jobs started with delays while we worked through the backlog.

From about 15:15 to 20:48 UTC, workflows and jobs started with increasing delays, of up to about an hour, and the CircleCI UI and API fell behind by up to about 2 hours. During this time, some jobs failed to start and some in-progress workflows failed.

From 20:48 to about 22:10 UTC, we temporarily paused starting new workflows and jobs so our systems could recover. New pipelines were accepted and queued during this time. From about 22:10 to 23:47 UTC, queued workflows and jobs resumed and were processed. Some of them had waited up to about 2 hours.

The issue has been resolved and all affected functionality has returned to normal. Usage charge data on the Project Usage page is not yet up to date and will be updated once our data backfills complete. Customers whose jobs failed during this window may rerun affected jobs. We thank you for your patience while our engineers worked on implementing a fix.

## Summary

Between 11:15 UTC and 23:47 UTC on October 9, CircleCI customers experienced hours-long delays and failures across pipelines, workflows and jobs, along with delays in the CircleCI UI, API and notifications.

* From 11:15 to 13:00 UTC, pipelines were created but not processed, and outbound webhooks and Slack and email notifications were not sent.
* From 13:00 to 14:40 UTC, workflows and jobs started with delays while we worked through the backlog.
* From 15:15 to 20:48 UTC, workflows and jobs started with increasing delays, of up to about an hour, and the CircleCI UI and API fell behind by up to about 2 hours. During this time, some jobs failed to start and some in-progress workflows failed.
* From 20:48 to 22:10 UTC, we temporarily paused starting new workflows and jobs so our systems could recover. New pipelines were accepted and queued during this time.
* From 22:10 to 23:47 UTC, queued workflows and jobs resumed and were successfully processed. Some of them had waited up to about 2 hours.
* By 23:47, the incident was mitigated.

The status page for this incident can be found at [October 9 - Delay in data appearing in UI and API](https://status.circleci.com/incidents/6cfhhlr4rmm0). Customers experienced a similar incident earlier in the week at [October 6 - Delays in pipelines, workflows, UI data, and notifications](https://status.circleci.com/incidents/z4hbq8h49j8c).

Multiple CircleCI services use Temporal backed by Postgres as a reliable queueing mechanism, and both incidents had the same cause: the rate of writes to Temporal's Postgres instance were faster than Postgres’s transaction log could archive those writes. In both cases, this caused multi-hour delays in processing both pipelines and status notifications.

We evaluated several mitigations, then paused new workflow starts so the system could recover safely, and ramped back up gradually. We then throttled work back up until our systems returned to normal.

To permanently resolve the bottleneck, we have split work across multiple Temporal instances, each with its own independent database and worker clusters, and we load-balance across them. We had already scheduled infrastructure work starting the week of October 12 that would have removed this exact bottleneck and prevented these incidents. So starting 19:11 on October 9 our engineering team implemented, tested, and rolled out a simpler version of these changes within a few hours. We further added new alerting and tuned the underlying databases for better performance under high load.

Customers whose jobs failed during this window may rerun them.

## Background

To run customer jobs, CircleCI executes a series of steps: we accept customer pipelines; we assign jobs for those pipelines to workers; we deliver status updates for those pipelines and jobs; and we charge customers for the credits those jobs consume. Each of these steps is implemented by an independent service, with reliable queues in between.

Historically we have implemented these reliable queues with RabbitMQ on top of durable storage, with exponential backoff and dead letter queues for reliability. Over the last year, we have increasingly reimplemented our reliable queues on [Temporal](https://temporal.io/), which provides far better durability and reliability guarantees over a simpler and more powerful programming model. Our build service \(which turns a pipeline config into an executable plan\), our workflow orchestrator service \(which distributes tasks onto workers\), our notification service \(which delivers status updates\), and our charging service \(which charges customers for credits\) all now use Temporal.

Temporal stores the state for its workflows and activities \(called “history”\) in a database, and this is the only component in a Temporal instance that is synchronous and stateful. As a consequence, a Temporal instance’s ability to accept and execute workflows is dependent on the write rate of its backing database. We have also configured Temporal to delete completed workflows and activities from its history 3 days after they complete.

At the time of this incident, we used a single clustered Temporal instance backed by a Multi-AZ Postgres RDS instance for all of these reliable queues. While a Multi-AZ RDS instance is resilient to zone failures, it maintains database consistency via a single write-ahead-log \(WAL\). At the time we had configured our Postgres instance to store its WAL on a Dedicated Log Volume \(DLV\) so log writes did not compete with data writes. The database archives the log continuously to backup storage, and it can only reuse space on the volume after the log has been archived. If the database writes logs faster than it archives, the volume fills and Postgres has no space to the write its WAL log. Then the database stops accepting incoming writes and goes entirely read-only. An RDS DLV is limited to 1TB of storage and 3000 IOPS and per AWS these limits are hardcoded and cannot be increased.

## What Happened

_\(All times UTC\)_

One of the contributing factors to the October 6 incident was that we were processing a high rate of Temporal history deletions at the same time as incoming work, which in turn put pressure on the backing database. To resolve the October 6 incident, we changed cleanup settings on Temporal’s largest tables and moved the transaction log back to its dedicated volume. These changes eliminated the major source of transaction log writes, but did not consider the additional log writes from scheduled deletions. Because we have configured Temporal to delete completed workflows and activities from its history 3 days after they complete, the October 6 history was scheduled to be deleted on October 9.

Starting at 08:00 on October 9, Temporal began processing those scheduled deletions, and as a consequence free space on the Postgres DLV began dropping precipitously, from 0.8TB at 08:00 to 0.1TB by 10:10. Our monitoring alerted at 10:28 and we declared an incident at 10:31. While our infrastructure team was investigating, at 11:15 the DLV ran out of space and the Postgres instance went read-only. This stopped all Temporal processing in its tracks.

At 11:42, we restarted Postgres to move the WAL log from the DLV onto the data volume and use the spare disk space and IOPS there. This maneuver had mitigated the incident on October 6, and we knew it would take roughly 60 minutes.

While the database was restarting, we began implementing several load-shedding techniques upstream of Temporal:

* We began investigating whether we should shed incoming workloads altogether to keep the rest moving, but ultimately decided that this would provide no value.
* At 12:29, we flagged off credit charging updates, which represented 12% of Temporal activities. This left the Pipeline Usage page with stale charging data, until we would backfill it, but would not lose data or prevent pipelines from running.

At 12:59, the database was back up and began processing work that had queued since 11:15 and by 14:40, this backlog had cleared and jobs were starting on time. However, by 15:15, delays returned as database’s routing cleanup had fallen far behind on the tables Temporal uses to track queued and scheduled work. Those tables normally hold tens of thousands of deleted rows awaiting cleanup, but by late afternoon, they held tens of millions of rows. Every Temporal operation had to read past those rows, so the database spent much more processing time on each one and Temporal ran slower. This resulted in customers continuing to see hour-long delays in starting pipelines and in status updates.

For the next several hours we attempted various mitigations, including:

* Manipulating Temporal configuration values to reduce database pressure. This had minimal effect.
* Running manual vacuum jobs to clean up dead rows in Postgres. This ended up competing for CPU with queries themselves, and was ultimately counterproductive. We cancelled them at 17:45 to relieve the pressure on the database load.
* We began trying to move all of the notification usecases to a separate Temporal instance. This represented 18% of Temporal activities. We successfully finished moving notifications by 17:07.
* At 17:16, we successfully implemented an optimization in our representation of pipeline state, which reduced it by 5%. That in turn reduced the size of database writes and therefore data pressure on the Postgres WAL log.

None of these fully mitigated the issue.

By 20:48, we realized that Postgres was now thrashing on database CPU and was no longer bottlenecked on log writes. We further realized that our upstream systems were both submitting new work and also retrying work that had earlier been submitted and failed. Recognizing that we were in a classic retry storm, we paused all incoming and retry work and let it queue up, in order to allow the database to fully complete in-process work. We then slowly throttled up queued work from 22:07 to keep the database at a sustainable load.

This fully succeeded by 23:47 when all queued work had started, and we closed the incident at 02:08 on October 10.

## Future Prevention and Process Improvement

### Multiple Temporal Instances

In parallel with incident mitigation and resolution, starting at 19:11 on October 9, we also began standing up multiple sharded Temporal instances and implementing the ability to load-balance incoming work between them.

Each of the multiple Temporal instances maintains its own independent database and worker clusters, and so is isolated from the others. As a postmortem action item from the October 6 incident, we had already scheduled infrastructure work that would have removed the bottleneck of a single Temporal instance and Postgres database, starting October 12 and expecting to take 2 weeks. On October 9, we realized that this work simply could not wait, so our engineering team implemented, tested, and rolled out a simpler version of the planned changes within a few hours.

These changes completed successfully at 01:45 on October 10.

**In addition, we are changing how we store and monitor transaction logs.** Our Temporal database no longer uses the fixed-size log volume. We are adding alerts on how far log archiving falls behind and how fast the database writes logs, so we can act hours earlier than we did on October 9.

**We are also revisiting the Temporal's deletion schedule.** Temporal deletes finished work a few days after it runs, so a busy day returns as database load later in the week. We are changing when and how quickly those deletions run.

**We are changing how our systems retry when Temporal is slow.** On October 9, our systems retried failed work against Temporal and added to its load. As we committed after the October 6 incident, we are changing our systems to wait for Temporal to recover so work is not dropped.

## Conclusion

Customer experience is our top priority, and we commit to continually improving the reliability of our systems to match the trust that our customers place in us. We thank our customers for their patience while our team worked to resolve these incidents.

Please reach out to our support team with any questions or concerns.

## Summary

Between 11:15 UTC and 23:47 UTC on October 9, CircleCI customers experienced hours-long delays and failures across pipelines, workflows and jobs, along with delays in the CircleCI UI, API and notifications.

* From 11:15 to 13:00 UTC, pipelines were created but not processed, and outbound webhooks and Slack and email notifications were not sent.
* From 13:00 to 14:40 UTC, workflows and jobs started with delays while we worked through the backlog.
* From 15:15 to 20:48 UTC, workflows and jobs started with increasing delays, of up to about an hour, and the CircleCI UI and API fell behind by up to about 2 hours. During this time, some jobs failed to start and some in-progress workflows failed.
* From 20:48 to 22:10 UTC, we temporarily paused starting new workflows and jobs so our systems could recover. New pipelines were accepted and queued during this time.
* From 22:10 to 23:47 UTC, queued workflows and jobs resumed and were successfully processed. Some of them had waited up to about 2 hours.
* By 23:47, the incident was mitigated.

The status page for this incident can be found at [October 9 - Delay in data appearing in UI and API](https://status.circleci.com/incidents/6cfhhlr4rmm0). Customers experienced a similar incident earlier in the week at [October 6 - Delays in pipelines, workflows, UI data, and notifications](https://status.circleci.com/incidents/z4hbq8h49j8c).

Multiple CircleCI services use Temporal backed by Postgres as a reliable queueing mechanism, and both incidents had the same cause: the rate of writes to Temporal's Postgres instance were faster than Postgres’s transaction log could archive those writes. In both cases, this caused multi-hour delays in processing both pipelines and status notifications.

We evaluated several mitigations, then paused new workflow starts so the system could recover safely, and ramped back up gradually. We then throttled work back up until our systems returned to normal.

To permanently resolve the bottleneck, we have split work across multiple Temporal instances, each with its own independent database and worker clusters, and we load-balance across them. We had already scheduled infrastructure work starting the week of October 12 that would have removed this exact bottleneck and prevented these incidents. So starting 19:11 on October 9 our engineering team implemented, tested, and rolled out a simpler version of these changes within a few hours. We further added new alerting and tuned the underlying databases for better performance under high load.

Customers whose jobs failed during this window may rerun them.

## Background

To run customer jobs, CircleCI executes a series of steps: we accept customer pipelines; we assign jobs for those pipelines to workers; we deliver status updates for those pipelines and jobs; and we charge customers for the credits those jobs consume. Each of these steps is implemented by an independent service, with reliable queues in between.

Historically we have implemented these reliable queues with RabbitMQ on top of durable storage, with exponential backoff and dead letter queues for reliability. Over the last year, we have increasingly reimplemented our reliable queues on [Temporal](https://temporal.io/), which provides far better durability and reliability guarantees over a simpler and more powerful programming model. Our build service \(which turns a pipeline config into an executable plan\), our workflow orchestrator service \(which distributes tasks onto workers\), our notification service \(which delivers status updates\), and our charging service \(which charges customers for credits\) all now use Temporal.

Temporal stores the state for its workflows and activities \(called “history”\) in a database, and this is the only component in a Temporal instance that is synchronous and stateful. As a consequence, a Temporal instance’s ability to accept and execute workflows is dependent on the write rate of its backing database. We have also configured Temporal to delete completed workflows and activities from its history 3 days after they complete.

At the time of this incident, we used a single clustered Temporal instance backed by a Multi-AZ Postgres RDS instance for all of these reliable queues. While a Multi-AZ RDS instance is resilient to zone failures, it maintains database consistency via a single write-ahead-log \(WAL\). At the time we had configured our Postgres instance to store its WAL on a Dedicated Log Volume \(DLV\) so log writes did not compete with data writes. The database archives the log continuously to backup storage, and it can only reuse space on the volume after the log has been archived. If the database writes logs faster than it archives, the volume fills and Postgres has no space to the write its WAL log. Then the database stops accepting incoming writes and goes entirely read-only. An RDS DLV is limited to 1TB of storage and 3000 IOPS and per AWS these limits are hardcoded and cannot be increased.

## What Happened

_\(All times UTC\)_

One of the contributing factors to the October 6 incident was that we were processing a high rate of Temporal history deletions at the same time as incoming work, which in turn put pressure on the backing database. To resolve the October 6 incident, we changed cleanup settings on Temporal’s largest tables and moved the transaction log back to its dedicated volume. These changes eliminated the major source of transaction log writes, but did not consider the additional log writes from scheduled deletions. Because we have configured Temporal to delete completed workflows and activities from its history 3 days after they complete, the October 6 history was scheduled to be deleted on October 9.

Starting at 08:00 on October 9, Temporal began processing those scheduled deletions, and as a consequence free space on the Postgres DLV began dropping precipitously, from 0.8TB at 08:00 to 0.1TB by 10:10. Our monitoring alerted at 10:28 and we declared an incident at 10:31. While our infrastructure team was investigating, at 11:15 the DLV ran out of space and the Postgres instance went read-only. This stopped all Temporal processing in its tracks.

At 11:42, we restarted Postgres to move the WAL log from the DLV onto the data volume and use the spare disk space and IOPS there. This maneuver had mitigated the incident on October 6, and we knew it would take roughly 60 minutes.

While the database was restarting, we began implementing several load-shedding techniques upstream of Temporal:

* We began investigating whether we should shed incoming workloads altogether to keep the rest moving, but ultimately decided that this would provide no value.
* At 12:29, we flagged off credit charging updates, which represented 12% of Temporal activities. This left the Pipeline Usage page with stale charging data, until we would backfill it, but would not lose data or prevent pipelines from running.

At 12:59, the database was back up and began processing work that had queued since 11:15 and by 14:40, this backlog had cleared and jobs were starting on time. However, by 15:15, delays returned as database’s routing cleanup had fallen far behind on the tables Temporal uses to track queued and scheduled work. Those tables normally hold tens of thousands of deleted rows awaiting cleanup, but by late afternoon, they held tens of millions of rows. Every Temporal operation had to read past those rows, so the database spent much more processing time on each one and Temporal ran slower. This resulted in customers continuing to see hour-long delays in starting pipelines and in status updates.

For the next several hours we attempted various mitigations, including:

* Manipulating Temporal configuration values to reduce database pressure. This had minimal effect.
* Running manual vacuum jobs to clean up dead rows in Postgres. This ended up competing for CPU with queries themselves, and was ultimately counterproductive. We cancelled them at 17:45 to relieve the pressure on the database load.
* We began trying to move all of the notification usecases to a separate Temporal instance. This represented 18% of Temporal activities. We successfully finished moving notifications by 17:07.
* At 17:16, we successfully implemented an optimization in our representation of pipeline state, which reduced it by 5%. That in turn reduced the size of database writes and therefore data pressure on the Postgres WAL log.

None of these fully mitigated the issue.

By 20:48, we realized that Postgres was now thrashing on database CPU and was no longer bottlenecked on log writes. We further realized that our upstream systems were both submitting new work and also retrying work that had earlier been submitted and failed. Recognizing that we were in a classic retry storm, we paused all incoming and retry work and let it queue up, in order to allow the database to fully complete in-process work. We then slowly throttled up queued work from 22:07 to keep the database at a sustainable load.

This fully succeeded by 23:47 when all queued work had started, and we closed the incident at 02:08 on October 10.

## Future Prevention and Process Improvement

### Multiple Temporal Instances

In parallel with incident mitigation and resolution, starting at 19:11 on October 9, we also began standing up multiple sharded Temporal instances and implementing the ability to load-balance incoming work between them.

Each of the multiple Temporal instances maintains its own independent database and worker clusters, and so is isolated from the others. As a postmortem action item from the October 6 incident, we had already scheduled infrastructure work that would have removed the bottleneck of a single Temporal instance and Postgres database, starting October 12 and expecting to take 2 weeks. On October 9, we realized that this work simply could not wait, so our engineering team implemented, tested, and rolled out a simpler version of the planned changes within a few hours.

These changes completed successfully at 01:45 on October 10.

**In addition, we are changing how we store and monitor transaction logs.** Our Temporal database no longer uses the fixed-size log volume. We are adding alerts on how far log archiving falls behind and how fast the database writes logs, so we can act hours earlier than we did on October 9.

**We are also revisiting the Temporal's deletion schedule.** Temporal deletes finished work a few days after it runs, so a busy day returns as database load later in the week. We are changing when and how quickly those deletions run.

**We are changing how our systems retry when Temporal is slow.** On October 9, our systems retried failed work against Temporal and added to its load. As we committed after the October 6 incident, we are changing our systems to wait for Temporal to recover so work is not dropped.

## Conclusion

Customer experience is our top priority, and we commit to continually improving the reliability of our systems to match the trust that our customers place in us. We thank our customers for their patience while our team worked to resolve these incidents.

Please reach out to our support team with any questions or concerns.

## What Happened

_\(All times UTC\)_

One of the contributing factors to the October 6 incident was that we were processing a high rate of Temporal history deletions at the same time as incoming work, which in turn put pressure on the backing database. To resolve the October 6 incident, we changed cleanup settings on Temporal’s largest tables and moved the transaction log back to its dedicated volume. These changes eliminated the major source of transaction log writes, but did not consider the additional log writes from scheduled deletions. Because we have configured Temporal to delete completed workflows and activities from its history 3 days after they complete, the October 6 history was scheduled to be deleted on October 9.

Starting at 08:00 on October 9, Temporal began processing those scheduled deletions, and as a consequence free space on the Postgres DLV began dropping precipitously, from 0.8TB at 08:00 to 0.1TB by 10:10. Our monitoring alerted at 10:28 and we declared an incident at 10:31. While our infrastructure team was investigating, at 11:15 the DLV ran out of space and the Postgres instance went read-only. This stopped all Temporal processing in its tracks.

At 11:42, we restarted Postgres to move the WAL log from the DLV onto the data volume and use the spare disk space and IOPS there. This maneuver had mitigated the incident on October 6, and we knew it would take roughly 60 minutes.

While the database was restarting, we began implementing several load-shedding techniques upstream of Temporal:

* We began investigating whether we should shed incoming workloads altogether to keep the rest moving, but ultimately decided that this would provide no value.
* At 12:29, we flagged off credit charging updates, which represented 12% of Temporal activities. This left the Pipeline Usage page with stale charging data, until we would backfill it, but would not lose data or prevent pipelines from running.

At 12:59, the database was back up and began processing work that had queued since 11:15 and by 14:40, this backlog had cleared and jobs were starting on time. However, by 15:15, delays returned as database’s routing cleanup had fallen far behind on the tables Temporal uses to track queued and scheduled work. Those tables normally hold tens of thousands of deleted rows awaiting cleanup, but by late afternoon, they held tens of millions of rows. Every Temporal operation had to read past those rows, so the database spent much more processing time on each one and Temporal ran slower. This resulted in customers continuing to see hour-long delays in starting pipelines and in status updates.

For the next several hours we attempted various mitigations, including:

* Manipulating Temporal configuration values to reduce database pressure. This had minimal effect.
* Running manual vacuum jobs to clean up dead rows in Postgres. This ended up competing for CPU with queries themselves, and was ultimately counterproductive. We cancelled them at 17:45 to relieve the pressure on the database load.
* We began trying to move all of the notification usecases to a separate Temporal instance. This represented 18% of Temporal activities. We successfully finished moving notifications by 17:07.
* At 17:16, we successfully implemented an optimization in our representation of pipeline state, which reduced it by 5%. That in turn reduced the size of database writes and therefore data pressure on the Postgres WAL log.

None of these fully mitigated the issue.

By 20:48, we realized that Postgres was now thrashing on database CPU and was no longer bottlenecked on log writes. We further realized that our upstream systems were both submitting new work and also retrying work that had earlier been submitted and failed. Recognizing that we were in a classic retry storm, we paused all incoming and retry work and let it queue up, in order to allow the database to fully complete in-process work. We then slowly throttled up queued work from 22:07 to keep the database at a sustainable load.

This fully succeeded by 23:47 when all queued work had started, and we closed the incident at 02:08 on October 10.

## Future Prevention and Process Improvement

### Multiple Temporal Instances

In parallel with incident mitigation and resolution, starting at 19:11 on October 9, we also began standing up multiple sharded Temporal instances and implementing the ability to load-balance incoming work between them.

Each of the multiple Temporal instances maintains its own independent database and worker clusters, and so is isolated from the others. As a postmortem action item from the October 6 incident, we had already scheduled infrastructure work that would have removed the bottleneck of a single Temporal instance and Postgres database, starting October 12 and expecting to take 2 weeks. On October 9, we realized that this work simply could not wait, so our engineering team implemented, tested, and rolled out a simpler version of the planned changes within a few hours.

These changes completed successfully at 01:45 on October 10.

**In addition, we are changing how we store and monitor transaction logs.** Our Temporal database no longer uses the fixed-size log volume. We are adding alerts on how far log archiving falls behind and how fast the database writes logs, so we can act hours earlier than we did on October 9.

**We are also revisiting the Temporal's deletion schedule.** Temporal deletes finished work a few days after it runs, so a busy day returns as database load later in the week. We are changing when and how quickly those deletions run.

Between 11:15 UTC and 23:47 UTC on October 9, customers experienced delays and failures across pipelines, workflows and jobs, along with delays in the CircleCI UI, API and notifications.

From 11:15 to about 13:00 UTC, pipelines were created but not processed, and outbound webhooks and Slack and email notifications were not sent. From about 13:00 to 14:40 UTC, workflows and jobs started with delays while we worked through the backlog.

From about 15:15 to 20:48 UTC, workflows and jobs started with increasing delays, of up to about an hour, and the CircleCI UI and API fell behind by up to about 2 hours. During this time, some jobs failed to start and some in-progress workflows failed.

From 20:48 to about 22:10 UTC, we temporarily paused starting new workflows and jobs so our systems could recover. New pipelines were accepted and queued during this time. From about 22:10 to 23:47 UTC, queued workflows and jobs resumed and were processed. Some of them had waited up to about 2 hours.

The issue has been resolved and all affected functionality has returned to normal. Usage charge data on the Project Usage page is not yet up to date and will be updated once our data backfills complete. Customers whose jobs failed during this window may rerun affected jobs. We thank you for your patience while our engineers worked on implementing a fix.

fields.title: Incident with Webhooks

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded performance for Webhooks
Pull Requests is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.
Issues is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.
Git Operations is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.
Packages is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.

We are currently investigating a brief degradation of service for Git operations (specifically pushes), issues, pull requests, package registry, and webhooks between 14:32 and 14:46 UTC. We have identified the source of the degradation and are investigating mitigation strategies to prevent recurrence.
The degradation affecting Git Operations, Issues, Packages, Pull Requests and Webhooks has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.
We have temporarily disabled a background job which caused the impact. At this time the impact is fully mitigated.

Between 14:24 and 14:53 UTC on 13 August 2026, a routine background job to delete an organization overwhelmed a key shared database, causing multiple GitHub services to briefly return elevated errors and slower responses. Most affected was the webhook management API, with smaller impact to Git operations, pull requests, issues, packages, sign-in, and Copilot. Impact cleared on its own at about 14:53 UTC once the job finished; we resolved the incident at 15:36 UTC.

Affected users may have experienced a brief increase in errors and slower responses, primarily when creating, listing, or updating webhooks, with smaller impacts to pull requests, issues, packages, and Git operations. Failures peaked at about 1% for several minutes around 14:37 UTC.

To prevent future incidents, we've already shipped an update that turns on the safer deletion path for organizations, along with caps on deletion holds on databases. Building on these changes, we're auditing all bulk deletion and cleanup jobs that write to shared databases to prevent similar issues in future.

fields.title: Incident with Actions and Pull Requests

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded performance for Actions and Pull Requests

We are investigating elevated delays and timeouts affecting Actions workflow runs triggered by pull request events. 20% of actions runs have delayed starts of more than 5 minutes and up to 4% of runs failed to trigger. We are actively working on mitigation and will provide updates as we learn more.
We've applied mitigations and are seeing recovery in Actions workflow runs and blocked pull request merges. We're continuing to monitor for sustained health of merge commit creates before resolving.
We confirmed full recovery beginning at 23:58 UTC. Actions workflow runs and pull request merges are operating normally. We will now resolve the incident while continuing to monitor service health.
The degradation affecting Actions and Pull Requests has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

On August 26, 2026, from 21:55 UTC to 23:58 UTC, 2.6% of workflow runs triggered by pull request events were delayed, with the impact rising as high as 25% at its peak. Some users also experienced delays in pull request merge-commit generation, mergeability information, and merge-button availability. Actions and Pull Requests fully recovered by 23:58 UTC; the incident was resolved at 00:26 UTC after normal operation was confirmed.

Background jobs that process pull request updates and generate merge commits were impacted by timeouts reaching a single partition of git data. This resulted in a backlog in pull request merge-commit processing, delaying pull request-triggered GitHub Actions workflows and some mergeability information.

We reduced workload, shifted traffic away from affected infrastructure, and restored the affected service component to a healthy state. Together, these actions helped drain the backlog and restore normal operations.

We are working to improve resource saturation detection and to eliminate customer impact in this scenario by isolating impact, placing better bounds on retries, and strengthening backpressure to make our systems more resilient under load.
